Mrs. Oliphant wrote The Doctor's Family as part of her Chronicles of Carlingford, in a new edition from William Blackwood and Sons. Young Dr. Rider lives in the new quarter of Carlingford, and his choice would shock any man chasing a reputation in society. A new house gazing over a brick-field interests him as much as an exclusive house in Grange Lane.

His own establishment shocks refined feeling. It is a corner house with a surgery round the corner. A red lamp gleams over half-formed streets and full brick-fields. A night-bell stands prominent, and his name sits on a staring brass plate. Friends advised the M.R.C.S. style, since folk there feared physicians and a guinea a visit. Oliphant builds a warm, sharp tale of a young doctor and a town's manners.
30086-has-anyone-here-seen-kelly:
Kenneth O'Hara tells a science fiction tale of Kelly, the stubborn human mind inside a communal Crew that sings, glows, and shares one life in a bed of protoplasm. Body tanks need refills and the ship needs service, yet the Crew drifts in a lotus dream and sees no need to check anything. Kelly insists on going out for a while, warning that they could run into something bad, while the Crew begs him to stay.

Paul Orban drew the pictures. The conflict is gentle rather than violent: the Crew loves Kelly, calls him its most interesting part, and wants his memories of Earth culture, only halfway through his life. Kelly, in turn, wants a ship that works and bodies that are sound. The short piece asks whether comfort shared by all is worth the watchfulness of one restless mind.
30362-paul-gerhardt-s-spiritual-songs-tr:
John Kelly translates a large selection from Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, published in London in 1867. Each piece appears in full, in the metre of the original. A biographical sketch and an index of first lines precede songs grouped by the church year and by theme.

Contents run from the Holy Trinity, Advent, and Christmas through Good Friday, Easter, and Whitsuntide. Later groups cover repentance, prayer, the Christian life, songs of the cross and consolation, praise, morning and evening songs, and death and eternal life. Kelly's versions aim for singable English that keeps Gerhardt's devotional voice, making a classic German hymn writer available to English readers.
30835-a-country-gentleman-and-his-family:
Mrs. Oliphant wrote this novel, published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1887, after a three-volume printing in 1886. Oliphant had already written The Wizard's Son and Hester, among others. Its hero, Theodore Warrender, is still at Oxford when his father dies, a youth who came up from school with the highest hopes for the university.

An admiring tutor had laid out his path with hopes that were almost certainties, if only he would work as he had worked for two years in the Sixth Form. When he and Brunson went up for scholarships, Brunson won and Warrender failed, to everyone's astonishment. His fine, fastidious mind had been carried away by an Aeschylus paper, turned into an exhaustive study of the famous beloved trilogy, to the neglect of other subjects. Oliphant follows a clever young man learning what failure and family duty mean.
32025-forget-me-nearly:
F. L. Wallace's short story Forget Me Nearly was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in June 1954. It opens in a police counselor's office, where Val Borgenese taps the small nameplate on his desk and asks the man across from him who he is. The man shakes his head and says indistinctly that he does not know.

Its headnote asks what sort of world it is that would not help victims find out whether they had been murdered or had committed suicide. Borgenese explains that names are difficult, like clothing put on or taken off, the first thing forgotten and the last remembered. Readers get a science-fiction mystery about identity, memory, and a man without a name.
32288-a-yankee-flier-in-italy:
Al Avery's A Yankee Flier in Italy, illustrated by Paul Laune and published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1944, is a Second World War air adventure for boys. Dedicated to Avon Kirks, its fourteen chapters run from Farewell Party and Special Task through Reunion, Beach-Head, and Prison Ship to Firing Squad, Rest Cure, Escape, and Homeward Bound. Lone Eagle, Rescue, Salerno, Night Raid, and Night Flight close the book.

The story opens at a farewell party about to break up, and not very successfully: Lieutenant O'Malley has devoured only one blueberry pie, which means he is feeling far from par. He sits sprawled in a big chair that had once been a Moslem prince's, his skinny legs extended. An illustration shows Stan snapping: We'll take over now. Readers get a wartime flier's tale of Italy, beach-heads, prison, and escape.
32336-maid-sally:
Harriet A. Cheever's novel, copyrighted in 1902, follows Sally, a young heroine first heard at Ingleside and later placed in a great house. Early chapters mix fairy-tale play, with a fairy town and a fairy prince, and a new Sally learning her place in a household. A supper company, a parson, and a long good-bye carry her from childhood games toward adult choices.

Later the story turns to a colonial ball, a soldier's card, the breaking of a storm, a campaign, and the Battle of Great Bridge. Sally faces war, separation, and questions about who she truly is, before a homecoming and a final meeting with her fairy prince. The book blends girlhood romance with the trials of colonial and wartime America.
32561-the-bramleighs-of-bishop-s-folly:
Charles James Lever's Bramleighs of Bishop's Folly, published in Boston in 1904 with illustrations by W. Cubitt Cooke and E. J. Wheeler, opens with a remarkable Bishop of Down in Ireland toward the close of the last century. A liberal in politics when liberalism lay close to disloyalty, he was splendidly hospitable when hospitality verged on recklessness. He carried opinions to extremes, with taste cultivated by foreign travel and an ample fortune for whims.

Having passed many years in Italy, the bishop loved that country, its people, and their mode of life, and built a folly that gives the novel its name. Lever, writing from Trieste in August 1868 to Alexander William Kinglake, dedicates the book to a friend whose genius and courage he admired. The novel follows the Bramleigh family through fortune, folly, and Irish society with Lever's usual wit.
32582-of-stegner-s-folly:
Richard S. Shaver's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1952, follows Old Professor Stegner, whose selective anti-gravitational field brought complications he never foresaw. The narrator, who knew the grand old man, insists Stegner never meant his blessing to become a curse to mankind, and that the catastrophe lay beyond all prophecy. Anyone living in 1972 inside Stegner's life-circle, he adds, would agree you can get too much of a good thing.

Stegner's device, after ten years of research, repelled some particles of matter while leaving others, reversing gravity for certain elements so they hurried away. Things got big, and too healthy, even a pumpkin growing beyond measure. Shaver's framing note says that when a twenty-foot goddess emerged from the jungle, people knew Stegner was serious. The tale turns a scientific blessing into runaway growth.
32635-the-diary-of-philip-westerly:
Paul Compton's The Diary of Philip Westerly, printed in Weird Tales in August and September 1936, is a brief tale of a man undone by his own reflection. Ten years after Philip Westerly vanished, leaving only a smashed mirror, his nephew gathers the story from the diary Westerly kept.

Westerly, wealthy, cruel, and selfish, loved mirrors and admired himself before a gigantic glass covering one wall of his room. One night his reflection stops following his movements, wears no tie, and shows a stubby beard and yellow fangs, and fear takes hold where vanity once stood.
32651-adolescents-only:
Irving Cox Jr. tells of Gary Elvin, a teacher of five years who boards with the Schermerhorn family. Their twin sons, husky blond tenth graders with a red convertible and a pool, throw parties that wear Elvin down. He counts eight hard months to June and dreams of a small college post.

Then a red flame falls from the sky, and Elvin finds a slim rocket less than five feet long in a field. Soon tenth graders turn a burner to gold, set a class afloat, and bend the town to their whims. Elvin must decide whether mass hypnosis, or something stranger, has seized his school.
3266-miss-billy:
Eleanor H Porter, author of Pollyanna, centers this novel on Billy, a girl arriving among relatives. Billy writes a letter first, and the strata, the family layers who will receive her, take shape around it. A telegram, getting ready, and the coming of Billy follow, with Spunk introduced and the room, and Billy herself, duly inspected.

A family conclave, Aunt Hannah, and Bertram with visitors fill the middle chapters. Cyril takes his turn, a surprise comes all around, and Aunt Hannah speaks her mind. Kate takes a hand as the story widens. Porter writes family feeling with warmth and wit, and Billy's arrival tests every household habit, gently and to everyone's good.
3292-the-clever-woman-of-the-family:
Charlotte M Yonge draws Rachel, the clever woman of the family, in this novel from the 1880 Macmillan edition. In search of a mission opens the book, with verses on refusing the daily round of useful, patient love. Rachel longs for some great emprise to prove her high spirit, and scorns the small duties her mother chooses for her.

The novel tests that scorn across a family story. A mother, sisters, and suitors press Rachel toward the ordinary heroism she despises, and events press harder. Yonge, moralist as ever, argues that the great deed may be the daily one done well. Readers who like Victorian family fiction with a sharp edge will find Rachel a heroine worth arguing with.
33264-living-up-to-billy:
Elizabeth Cooper's novel is told in letters, opening with a note to Kate, who has just heard a judge give her two years after being caught with stolen goods. The letter writer, who sat through the trial, marvels that the term was no longer, given Kate's record. From that sharp start, the story follows Kate and those around her as they try to live up to Billy, a figure whose name sets the standard for the whole tale.

Copyrighted in 1915, the book mixes humor, slang, and feeling in the voice of its letter writers. Its scenes move between court, home, and street, and its charm lies in frank talk and quick character sketches. Readers who enjoy an epistolary novel with a lively, early twentieth-century voice will find here a brisk and warm story.
33479-the-opium-monopoly:
Ellen N. La Motte's Opium Monopoly, published in 1920, exposes the system by which governments profited from opium, with illustrations drawn from the trade's history. La Motte, a nurse and writer who knew Asia well, argues that the monopoly harmed peoples while filling treasuries, and her book belongs to the campaign against the drug trade. Its tone is moral, factual, and urgent.

The volume suits readers of drug and colonial history, offering a contemporary case against a policy defended by revenue. Its detail on trade, addiction, and official complicity remains striking. For students of the opium question, it is a key source: a woman's clear, angry account of a monopoly that history has judged a shame.
33775-little-robins-learning-to-fly:
A volume in A. R. Baker's Robin Redbreast series, this small book follows young robins as they learn to fly. The nestlings, first safe in the robins' nest, must try their wings, leave the familiar branches, and discover the air, the garden, and the dangers and delights beyond. Short, simple episodes suit very young readers, with gentle lessons in courage, patience, and family care tucked inside the birds' progress.

As one of several Robin books covering the nest, trouble, friends, and love one to another, this volume belongs to the same nineteenth-century children's world as the Little Frankie series. Families reading aloud will enjoy its tender pace and its belief that growing up, for birds as for children, takes practice, encouragement, and a safe place to return to.
33836-the-new-conspiracy-against-the-jes:
R. C. Dallas detects and briefly exposes a new conspiracy against the Jesuits in this 1815 London volume. Dedicated to George Canning, ambassador to Portugal, the book quotes the Jesuit institute's call to solid virtues and spiritual study. It also quotes Robertson's remark that the causes of the order's ruin deserve every intelligent observer's attention.

Dallas defends the Society of Jesus against its critics and warns that schooling cut loose from religion threatens social order. The volume preserves an early nineteenth-century Catholic apologetic, written in the years after the order's restoration. It offers historians a partisan but detailed view of anti-Jesuit polemic, Jesuit self-description, and the politics of religious education in post-Napoleonic Europe.
3431-the-gadfly:
Ethel Lilian Voynich sets this novel of revolution in Italy, opening in the library of a theological seminary at Pisa. Arthur, a sensitive young student, sits among manuscript sermons on a hot June evening, and his faith, his friendships, and his love soon collide with secret politics. The author thanks libraries and archives in Florence and Bologna for help with the Italian background.

Arthur reappears years later as the Gadfly, a bitter satirist who mocks priests and rulers in print while working for a revolutionary cause. The novel follows betrayal, disguise, and sacrifice toward a tragic end. It became famous far beyond Italy, and it suits readers who like passionate stories of faith, politics, and personal vengeance.
35045-the-hazeley-family:
Johnson wrote The Hazeley Family, a tale for young readers printed at Philadelphia in 1894 by a Baptist press. She was known for Clarence and Corinne. The tale starts in the Hazeley home, with Flora at its heart, and brings in Ruth Rudd in an early chapter.

Flora's first Sunday starts a chain of change, with results tracked chapter by chapter. Visits, a hospital stay, and a new home for Ruth widen the tale. Trials for Lottie Piper and a homely wedding come late. The book closes with a Christmas call. Young readers get a warm tale of faith, home, and growth, told in short, clear parts.
36433-chronicles-of-the-schonberg-cotta-:
Two members of the family tell the Chronicles of the Schonberg-Cotta Family, a work of religious fiction set in the age of Luther. The publisher's note explains the design: to bring the times of the Reformation before the reader more vividly than plain history can. The diary form does the work.

One branch of the Cotta family were Luther's earliest and closest friends. Family members record their daily life as the great events unfold around them, so readers seem to hear Luther and his circle speak. The publisher warns that the diary is invented, though built on accredited history. The book was a Victorian best seller, and it taught many English readers their picture of Luther's world.
36642-eli-s-children-the-chronicles-of-a:
Eli's Children, The Chronicles of an Unhappy Family, is a novel by George Manville Fenn. The hosted edition was published in London and dated in its front matter to eighteen eighty two. Part one is called The Rectory Folk and opens in a place named Lawford. Hot water in Lawford is the first chapter's own head, promising village trouble at once.

A deaf, bent old man is teased by a speaker who roars at him in the opening scene. Fenn builds a family chronicle around a rectory household and its sorrows, as the subtitle warns. Village talk, stubborn age, and young pride clash in dialogue led scenes. Fenn wrote scores of such tales for family reading.
36827-the-vulture-maiden-die-geier-wally:
Wilhelmine von Hillern wrote The Vulture Maiden, a tale of the Tyrolean Alps first told in German as Die Geier-Wally. Bell and Poynter translated it, and the Tauchnitz edition came out at Leipzig in 1876. Hillern dedicated the book to Berthold Auerbach, the famed writer of German village tales.

High in the Oetz valley, a lone maiden stands on a cliff above a roaring gorge. Guides point her out to travelers as the Vulture Maiden, since no other girl would dare those heights. Chapters follow her hard path: she is unbending, cast out, and sent back to her father. Names like Joseph the bear hunter and old Luckard fill the tale. The story mixes mountain scenery with a strong-willed heroine's fight for her own life.
37118-concerning-sally:
William John Hopkins wrote this novel, published in Boston and New York in 1912. Hopkins had already written The Indian Book, The Meddlings of Eve, and other tales. The story opens not with Sally but with a professor at his desk.

Professor Ladue sits in his room, looking out at trees turning from green to copper and gold. A river winds below and hills rise in the distance, yet he sees none of it. A slight smile, not a pleasant one, sits on his face as he eyes his papers and a skull on his desk. Something in his settled life is about to stir. Readers get a quiet, well-observed novel in Hopkins's calm, exact style.
37144-observations-on-madness-and-melanc:
Observations on Madness and Melancholy is a sick lore book by John Haslam, a drug man of a great mad house of London. This is its next form, much grown, out in eighteen nine. It holds use notes on those ills, with cases, and a count of the sick marks found past death cuts. A line past a famed wit heads it, on the dread of the loss of sense.

Haslam says the rise of mad ill has spurred past men to probe it, some for lore and some for gain. Past ten years had run past his first small work on the theme. This book is that work set right and much grown past his years at the great house. He calls it a short sum of long watch and work in a post rich in chance to see the ill.
37321-remarks-on-a-pamphlet-lately-publi:
Remarks on a Pamphlet is John Harrison's printed defence of his longitude watch. Sandby published the second edition in London in 1767. It cost sixpence. Harrison answers a pamphlet by Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal. That pamphlet appeared under the Board of Longitude's authority. The quarrel concerned the great longitude prize.

Harrison charges suppression and misrepresentation of facts. Maskelyne's tables, he says, confuse the ordinary reader. Conclusions would be taken on trust unless publicly contradicted. Harrison promises to avoid terms of art. He then explains longitude for the layman. The earth is divided into 360 degrees. Its daily turn brings each degree under the sun in turn. Four minutes of time answer to one degree sailed.
37692-cathedral-cities-of-italy:
Collins's Cathedral Cities of Italy, written and illustrated by Collins himself, was published in London in 1911 by William Heinemann, with Dodd, Mead in New York. A plate of St Peter's, Rome, stands near the front. Companion volumes on the cathedral cities of England, France, and Spain are advertised at the front, at sixteen shillings net, each with sixty reproductions from water-colours.

The contents run down the peninsula and up again: Como, Milan, Pavia, Bergamo, Brescia, Verona, Padua, and Venice at length. Rimini, Ferrara, Ravenna, Bologna, and Parma follow, then Genoa, Pisa, and Lucca, with Florence given the longest run of pages and Perugia after. The book's plan is uniform with its companions: short town essays built around the pictures.
38188-amusement-only:
Richard Marsh wrote a set of short tales printed in London in 1901 under the title Amusement Only. Marsh was known for The Beetle and The Seen and the Unseen. The tales are made for light reading, as the title owns with a smile. Yet most of them turn on crime, loss, or a strange turn of fate.

The first tale, The Lost Duchess, opens when a carriage comes home without the duchess who should ride in it. The coachman and footman can give no clear account. Other tales tell of strange events in Canterstone Jail, twins, a night vision, and a maid and a man. Each tale is short and ends with a twist.
38684-parson-kelly:
Mason and Andrew Lang wrote Parson Kelly, a tale printed in New York and London in 1899. A front print shows a man grieved that he has no Virgil. The book is given to Baron Tanneguy de Wogan, of an old house gay in exile and firm in loyalty.

The tale rests on the deeds of his kin, the Chevalier Nicholas de Wogan, a Jacobite agent. Parson Kelly speaks fine words at the Mazarin Palace to open the plot. Wogan must shun a bad acquaintance in a London street and teach the parson the ways of women. Fans of tales of intrigue get plots, Latin peril, and critics in a gay, swift tale.
38735-highways-and-byways-in-cambridge-a:
Reverend Edward Conybeare wrote this travel book on Cambridge and Ely, published in London in 1910. Conybeare had already written a history of the county and a book of rides around Cambridge. Pictures by Frederick Griggs run through the text.

The first chapter walks the green Backs of the colleges and traces the town from Roman times. Conybeare tells of Danes, Normans, old religious houses, and the rise of the university. Later chapters roam the roads and fens toward Ely and its great cathedral. Readers get a warm, learned guide to a small corner of England, written by a man who knew its lanes well.
39367-the-catholic-world-vol-01-april-to:
The Catholic World, Volume One, gathers the first six numbers of a monthly eclectic magazine, from April to September 1865. Lawrence Kehoe published it at New York. The Catholic World called itself a magazine of general literature and science. Its contents range far beyond sermons, as a first volume should.

Ancient saints of God and a pilgrimage to Ars open the list. The Christian schools of Alexandria take two long papers. Recent discoveries in the catacombs and Cardinal Wiseman in Rome follow. The marquis de Chastellux, the workings of the Holy Spirit in the Church of England, and Cochin China fill out the eclecticism. The volume appeared in the month the Civil War ended, founding what became America's long-lived Catholic review. A bookseller's fine-binding note at the front shows the set was made to be kept, bound in Toronto for Canadian readers.
40381-vistas-in-sicily:
Vistas in Sicily is a travel book by Arthur Stanley Riggs, published in New York in 1912. It belongs to a series called the Blue Books of Travel. Some chapters first appeared in the Travel Magazine. Riggs admits he and his wife knew almost nothing of Sicily before going. Sicily in spring struck them like water in the desert. Their vague notions came from wearisome school geography.

Eighteen chapters tour the island in a wide circuit. Palermo and its cathedrals and palaces come first. The plain of Panormos and a circuit of the island follow. The road to Syracuse leads to the harbour and the river Anapo. Catania and Mount Etna get a chapter, as does Taormina. Mountain vistas and the northern and western shores close the tour. A list of the best books on Sicily and an index end the volume.
40408-a-devotee-an-episode-in-the-life-o:
A Devotee is a novel by Cholmondeley, author of past tales of a storm girl and of a knights house. This is its second form, put out at London and New York in the late eighteen nineties. All rights were kept. Its full head calls it a brief span in the life of a frail, gay thing of the world.

Its gift word makes it out to a friend, on whose kind strong hand the pen has so oft leant. A verse at its head vows that a day is sure, though not this week nor month nor year. That day, great love shall be clean lost to mind, while poor soft love shall still hold out. Its first scene fills a great church with sound and heads.
40621-little-tony-of-italy:
Little Tony of Italy is a children's travel story by Madeline Brandeis. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York. The copyright dates to 1934. Photographs illustrate nearly every page. Brandeis dedicated the book to her mother. Her mother's singing, she writes, tunes with the singing land of Italy.

The contents follow Tony across the country. Tony and Tina open the tale in Naples. The Balilla, the fascist youth corps, enters the story early. Chapters visit Rome and its great sights. Photographs show Saint Peter's, the Colosseum, and the Trevi Fountain. A buried city chapter takes the children to Pompeii. Fever and troubled sleep threaten the journey. A pronouncing vocabulary closes the book.
40673-the-tiger-lily:
George Manville Fenn wrote the novel Tiger Lily, which opens in a rich, old fashioned bedroom on a bright morning. A sharp faced man named Masters lies in a great four post bed, in pain, and snaps at his barber. A calm doctor, Thorpe, comes in and gets a rough greeting from his patient.

The first chapter, called Modern Skill, sets the quarrel of tempers that drives the tale. Masters mocks the doctor, dares him to cut his hair the next day if he still lives, and shows a wit as sharp as his pain. Fenn builds a story of sickness, skill, and strong wills from that bedside clash.
41165-the-isles-of-scilly:
Jessie Mothersole painted and described The Isles of Scilly: Their Story, Their Folk and Their Flowers, for the Religious Tract Society at London. The second edition of 1914 answers many requests for a cheaper form, the first of 1910 having sold out. Cromwell's Castle on Tresco fronts the book.

Mothersole calls her pages an artist's impressions, in colour and in ink, with the history the unwritten law of colour-books requires. Chapters cover the islands' story, their former industries and the flower industry that replaced them, and the island folk and their ways. Stories of the wrecks follow, then Annet and its sea-birds, and the islands one by one: St Mary's, Tresco, Bryher and Samson, St Agnes and St Martin's with its neighbours.
41433-robert-kimberly:
Frank Spearman wrote this novel of love and high finance, and Scribner published it in February nineteen eleven. James Montgomery Flagg drew the pictures. The scene is the Lake country, at a quiet casino called the Hickories, with fields for golf and polo near by.

Alice comes as a guest and finds the place calm, almost too calm. Robert Kimberly, a man of wealth and force, stands at the heart of the tale. A woman's voice in the frontispiece cries that she scorns a threat, and the clash of pride and love drives the plot. Church scenes, songs, and hard words at close range give the book its heat. Spearman mixes romance with the world of deals and rail power.
41660-a-fortnight-of-folly:
A Fortnight of Folly is a tale by Maurice Thompson, printed in 1888. Street and Smith of New York and London later held the rights. Thompson had writ Alice of Old Vincennes among his earlier books. The volume also holds Hugh Conway's Tale of a Sculptor inside. Carriston's Gift stands as the third piece in the small book here.

The Hotel Helicon stood on a rock promontory in the southern mountains. A Cincinnati man built it new, rich from natural gas speculations. He made the house famous by rare liberality. From the valley it looked like a huge white bird at rest. Broad verandas and green Venetian shutters faced the visitor on arrival. Fresh-cut stumps and scarcely dry paint marked the newness of all. A whole day of hard zig-zag climbing brought guests to its door. Springs sang down little ravines toward a silver river thread.
41700-hi-jolly:
Jim Kjelgaard, the beloved writer of dog and wilderness stories, wrote this tale of the Army's camel experiment, published in New York in 1960 with pictures by Kendall Rossi. Its note warns that the setting and many events rest on history, though the people are imagined. It opens with Ali finding his camel.

Ali is the camel driver the soldiers called Hi Jolly, a Syrian cameleer hired to handle the camels the Army imported for desert freight in the Southwest. Chapters run from ambush to pilgrimage as man and beasts cross a strange new desert. Readers get a true, odd corner of Western history told for young readers.
43037-guy-kenmore-s-wife-and-the-rose-an:
Guy Kenmore Wife and The Rose and the Lily is a double volume of love tales in the Eagle Series, sold for ten cents as number 198. The series list credits the book to McVeigh Miller. Two full tales stand back to back in one cheap volume.

The first tale, Guy Kenmore Wife, bears the second title Her Mother Secret and runs to fifty two chapters. The second tale, The Rose and the Lily, bears the second title Love Wins Love and runs to twenty eight chapters. Both were sold in the Street and Smith line of copyright romances for news stands. Readers of dime love fiction got two whole novels for a dime, each full of secrets, hearts, and trials of love.
43330-harper-s-young-people-november-2-1:
Harper's Young People for November 2, 1880 is a children's weekly issue. Harper and Brothers of New York put the paper out each Tuesday. It stands as volume two, number 53 of the sheet. Four cents bought a copy, a dollar fifty the year in advance. Bits of Advice by Aunt Marjorie Precept opens the number.

Answer an invitation promptly and say if you can come, she writes. Name your boat or train and your hour of leaving home as well. A week is the usual length to assume for a friendly visit. Stay no longer unless urged, or you wear out your welcome fast. The most agreeable guest is the one regretted when he goes away. Be pleased with what is done for you, and say so. Charlie ran to help Tom's mother with a gate. Tales and pictures fill the rest.
43357-harper-s-young-people-november-9-1:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, November 9, 1880, came out at New York at four cents a copy and a dollar fifty a year. Volume two, number fifty four opens with a work of art drawn by Jessie Curtis. A poem on the jack o' lantern by Mary Folsom leads the number. Who is this nabob come to town after a long vacation, she asks.

He seems to have a host of friends and makes a great sensation. He stalks about these frosty nights while troops of boys run after him with merry jests and laughter. All summer long he lay forlorn and neglected on the ground. But see him now, with head aloft in regal splendor. A Lafayette and Washington tale stands within, of the young Frenchman's first meeting with the general at Philadelphia. Stories, verses, and pictures fill a famous boys' and girls' weekly.
43442-the-golden-butterfly:
Walter Besant and James Rice wrote this novel together, and dedicated it to Edmund Yates of The World. That paper first published the story in serial form. In their preface the authors explain the odd thing that gives the book its name and its start.

An English traveller had seen a golden butterfly kept as a curiosity in a mining city near Sacramento. The freak of nature was real, they insist, not their invention. The same traveller, Edgar Besant, gave them the account behind their Empire City scenes. California gold country, chance and a strange insect set the tale in motion.
4354-by-the-ionian-sea-notes-of-a-ramble:
George Gissing wrote this travel book from a ramble in southern Italy, along the Ionian Sea. He opens at Naples on a third day of sirocco, heavy-clouded and sunless, longing for mountains and sea. The next day he plans to take the Messina boat, calling at Paola, a place he has imagined for more than a year.

Later chapters visit Taranto, Cotrone, Catanzaro, Squillace, and Reggio, with the grave of Alaric, the table of the paladins, and faces by the way. Gissing writes as a literary traveler, fond of history and of poor southern towns. The book gives a slower Italy than the tourist's, seen on foot and by coastal boat.
43607-builders-of-united-italy:
Rupert Sargent Holland wrote Builders of United Italy, published in New York in 1908 with eight portraits. His subject is the long struggle of the scattered Italian states to become one nation, a story he calls by turns desperate and hopeful.

Holland gives one life to each force in that struggle: Alfieri the poet, Manzoni the man of letters, and Gioberti the philosopher. Then come Manin of Venice, Mazzini the prophet, Cavour the statesman, Garibaldi the crusader, and King Victor Emmanuel. Each portrait shows how words, plots, diplomacy, and war each did part of the work of unification.
44114-a-jay-of-italy:
Bernard Capes set this romance in the Italy of 1476. Methuen published it at London in 1905. Four editions came out between July and October of that year, a swift success.

The title quotes Cymbeline: a jay of Italy, whose mother was her painting, betrayed him. Carlo Lanti halts at an inn on the Milan road. His lady rides beside him on a white palfrey, her bridle bells tinkling. Lanti calls for wine with an oath. Capes paints him plainly: a bully and a spendthrift, yet good-humored under thick black brows. Falcons, pages, and tentmen crowd the road behind.
44279-harper-s-young-people-december-7-1:
Harper's Young People is an illustrated weekly paper for children, dated December 1880. Harper and Brothers published it in New York. The price was four cents a copy. This is number 58 of volume two. A drawing by Rogers fronts the issue. It shows Toby striking a bargain at a circus booth. The lead story is Toby Tyler, by James Otis.

Toby Tyler tells of ten weeks with a circus. Toby is a very small boy with big, staring eyes. He haggles for peanuts at a candy stand. Six nuts for a cent is the vendor's hard rate. A bad nut wins him two more in trade. The circus has just come to the town of Guilford. Posters have filled the boy's head for days. Otis made Toby a favourite of young readers. The tale ran here in weekly parts.
44311-corleone-a-tale-of-sicily:
Marion Crawford wrote this novel of Sicily, copyrighted in 1896 and reprinted at London and New York in 1905. It belongs to his Saracinesca world. The tale opens in talk between two brothers: Ippolito Saracinesca teases his elder brother Orsino that a man who never means to marry might as well turn priest. Orsino takes the joke without a smile.

From that cool start the story moves into Sicilian family pride, love, and violence, in the town that gives the book its name. Crawford knew Italy deeply and set many of his best novels there. Corleone stands among his most read tales of the South. Readers get a vivid, old-world Sicily of honour and vendetta, drawn by an American who lived in it.
44597-harper-s-young-people-january-18-1:
Harper Young People for Tuesday, January 18, 1881 is volume two, number sixty four of the pictured weekly for youth. Harper and Brothers put it out in New York at four cents a copy. A plate of Dutch sleigh riding stands at the front.

The lead tale, Who Got the Mitten, is by Rose Terry Cooke. It opens with a letter in broad dialect from John Jackson to Roxy Blair. John has had many calls for mittens this winter, and asks Roxy to knit two threaded ones for drovers, on commission. Roxy lays down her glasses and laughs at John gumption. She has twenty runs of blue yarn and some red spun last year. The issue mixes tales, facts, and fun for young readers of 1881.
44637-brother-billy:
Brother Billy is a story for young readers by Frances Margaret Fox, first printed in 1904 and issued at Boston in 1905. Fox also wrote Farmer Brown and the Birds and Betty of Old Mackinaw. The book has pictures by Etheldred B. Barry and was sold in the Cosy Corner line of tales for children.

Chapter heads point to visits from Aunt Florence, days of swimming, a steam tug named Billy, and tales told by Antoine Lebrinn. Later chapters bring ice fishing and Christmas Eve. The tale keeps a warm home tone, mixing outdoor fun, tall tales, and family life for its young hero and those around him.
44650-harper-s-young-people-january-4-18:
Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly from Harper and Brothers of New York, issued its number for Tuesday, January 4, 1881. It is the sixty-second number of the second volume, at four cents, or a dollar and a half a year. A picture, drawn by Yeager from a sketch by Taylor, shows fishing through the ice. The number opens with Mr Chalker's Ruse, by Frank Taylor.

That tale sets a New England village school-house on the bleakest hill, where the stove roasts the scholars near it and leaves the rest to freeze. On the coldest morning of the winter the mill-pond, smooth for shinny, tempts the boys away. Mr Chalker, the schoolmaster, walks his room of empty desks, with three boys huddled by the stove. The paper fed boys and girls tales, pictures, and facts.
44652-harper-s-young-people-january-11-1:
Harper Young People of January eleventh, eighteen eighty one, is a week sheet for youth. Year two, sheet sixty three, stands on its front leaf in print. Price was four cents, or a dollar half for the year in paid front. A front cut shows John Milton at age ten in his youth. The lead piece tells the youth of Milton for young eyes in plain words.

Milton was a fair haired Saxon boy, born in Bread Street in sixteen nine. His sire made wealth as a writ clerk and loved books and tune. Late night study at age twelve dimmed the boy sight in that house. Shakespeare and Jonson may have passed him on that street in his youth. Paul school made him one of its best wits in those days.
44712-harper-s-young-people-january-25-1:
Harper's Young People, volume two, number sixty-five, is an illustrated weekly for the young dated Tuesday, 25 January 1881. Harper and Brothers of New York published it at four cents a copy. Its lead serial is Toby Tyler, or Ten Weeks with a Circus, by James Otis. The chapter here, An Accident and Its Consequences, had begun in an earlier number.

Toby sells goods at the circus and takes no more bad money that evening. Mr Jacobs scolds and swears by turns, and lets Toby think he does half the work he should, though the boy surprises him at selling. Toby's private hoard grows by ninety cents in presents, and he feels almost a rich man. He hopes to visit his friends the skeleton and the fat woman before the night ride. The frontispiece shows the breakdown and escape of the monkeys.
44753-harper-s-young-people-february-1-1:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, February 1, 1881, is number 66 of volume two of Harper and Brothers' illustrated weekly for children. The catalog gives the year as 1881. The issue cost four cents, or a dollar and a half a year in advance.

A poem called Kitty's First Pie opens the number. Kitty bakes her pie herself in a patty pan, flaky and light, from a recipe in her mother's big book with advice from the cook. Bertha her sister, little dog Buff, and a cat named Mrs Purr will help eat it. Stories, verses, and pictures in that vein fill the weekly. Harper's Young People taught and amused a generation of American children. This issue is a fair spoonful of its fare.
44768-harper-s-young-people-february-8-1:
Harper's Young People was an illustrated weekly for children, and this issue is volume two, number sixty-seven, dated Tuesday, February 8, 1881. Harper and Brothers published it in New York at four cents a copy, or a dollar fifty a year. A front picture shows an attack in a mountain pass.

The number leads with Muffled, a story by William Stoddard. Two wagon men, the Irishman Pat Linihan and the grizzled Rube, camp in a hollow that may be the Chico Valley. Rube warns that the place is a bad boarding-house for white men, with hostile Indians near. Even the mules, Governor and Senator, get their characters read. Such weeklies mixed adventure tales, pictures, and instruction for the young readers of the Gilded Age.
44925-harper-s-young-people-february-15-:
Harper's Young People is an illustrated weekly paper for the young, and this is its issue of Tuesday, February 15, 1881. It is volume two, number 68, published by Harper and Brothers in New York at four cents a copy. A picture of perilous coasting heads the front page.

The issue opens with a story, A Ripper, by William Stoddard. Two gangs of boys, the West Hill coasters and the East Hill boys, face off over a new coasting machine. It is nothing, one scoffs, but a pair of bobs, a plank rigged across two sleds. The leader of the West Hill boys insists no one ever showed his hill how to make a ripper like this one. The talk runs on steering, rudders, and heels dug in as brakes, the whole pride of winter sport on two rival hills.
44927-harper-s-young-people-february-22-:
An issue of Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for children. Harper and Brothers published it at New York. This number is dated Tuesday, February 22, 1881. It belongs to volume two as number sixty-nine. The price was four cents, or a dollar fifty a year. An engraving of an ice-boat race fronts the issue.

The lead story is How the Pennant Was Won, by J O Davidson. Snowballs wake Arthur before dawn one freezing morning. His friend Joe brings splendid news at the window. The river has frozen clear to Tarrytown, and ice-boats will race today. Better still, the dominie lies ill, so school is cancelled. Uncle Nye's new yacht Jack Frost needs the boys as crew. Such numbers mixed sport, stories, and science for young readers.
44942-harper-s-young-people-december-21-:
Harper and Brothers issued Harper's Young People as a weekly paper with pictures for the young. Volume two, number sixty is dated Tuesday, December twenty-one, eighteen eighty. The price was four cents a copy, or a dollar and a half a year. A Christmas picture fronts this holiday number.

A short play by Edgar Fawcett leads the issue. When the Clock Struck Twelve is a Christmas play in one act. It is set in the castle of a rich French nobleman around sixteen hundred. His son Henri is twelve, and his daughter Lucienne is ten. Servants and a maid complete the small cast. The play brings a touch of old France to a family Christmas.
44943-harper-s-young-people-march-1-1881:
Harpers Young People is a drawn week sheet for the young. This is its print for the first of March in eighteen eighty-one. It is volume two of the sheet, at the price of a few coins the print. A plate of a boy of the old book heads the first tale. That tale, by a church chief, tells of that boy in a small town of the east of old.

A crowd fills the town square past two guests with strange news of a king born past fifty years. Those guests tell of deeds of grace and of a death past which that king came back to life. One guest fixes his eyes on a lame man, born so, and bids him stand on his feet. The man leaps and walks at once. The crowd cries that gods have come down in the form of men.
44981-harper-s-young-people-march-8-1881:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for children, printed in New York by Harper and Brothers. The issue of Tuesday, March 8, 1881, is volume two, number seventy-one, priced at four cents. A picture of sugaring off, drawn by Yeager, fills the front page.

A story by William Stoddard leads the number. A sleigh full of young people rides to old Mr Wire's maple sugar camp. Their city cousin Jerry boasts that he knows all about sugar. The March thaw has just begun, and the sleighing is fine. The tale promises a lesson for the boaster among the sap buckets. The issue shows the mix of story, picture, and country lore the paper offered each week.
45152-harper-s-young-people-march-15-188:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, March 15, 1881, is one issue of an illustrated weekly for children. Harper and Brothers published it in New York at four cents a copy. This is volume two, number seventy two, as the head of the issue states.

The number carries chapter fourteen of Toby Tyler, or Ten Weeks with a Circus, by James Otis. Mr Castle teaches Toby to ride in the ring in this part. A broad wooden saddle, a long whip, and a strange belt rig puzzle the boy. The tale had begun in the issue of December 7. Other stories, poems, and pictures fill the weekly around it. Readers get a warm sample of a loved children's paper.
45193-harper-s-young-people-march-22-188:
Harper Young People for March the twenty second 1881 is an issue of an illustrated weekly. Harper and Brothers of New York sold the paper at four cents a number. Volume two, number seventy three, is the full marking on the masthead of this issue. A drawing called The Luck of the Horseshoe heads the opening story.

Tommy Tucker Horseshoe, by Mrs Frank McCarthy, leads the fiction in this number. Tommy lives on a city farm near Central Park that scoffers call the sunken lots. Squatter jokes do not touch the boy, whose family was happy for a long run. How luck turns, and how a child learns misery from joy, drive the tale.
45194-harper-s-young-people-march-29-188:
Harper’s Young People for March twenty ninth, eighteen hundred eighty one, is an illustrated weekly for the young. Harper and Brothers sold the issue for four cents a copy. It is volume two, number seventy four. A year of the paper cost one dollar and fifty cents in advance.

Howard Pyle leads with The Magic Wand, a tale of old Wilmington. Dutch Dolly Vertz sold greens from her truck patch there. Her small husband cut clothes cross-legged at his bench. Dolly held the purse and kept him short of coin. He told fortunes by the stars to earn stray cents. Two boys, Ned Springer and Billy Shallcross, hung on his tall tales. Pyle draws the quaint Quaker town with warm care.
45196-harper-s-young-people-april-5-1881:
Harper Young People for 5 April 1881 is an illustrated weekly for the young, issued in New York. Harper and Brothers published the number at four cents, or a dollar and a half a year in advance. It is volume two, number seventy five, of the run. 

The first story, The Blackbirds Nest by Mary Cecil Hay, opens in a wood path. Jim has taken a nest, and Ned pleads with him to put it back at once. Ned warns that they are in sight of the Master, and Jim takes him to mean the squire of the estate. Ned meant a higher Master, and Jim sneers at the Sunday school stuff of his friend. The tale turns on whether the birds home, as much a home as any cottage, will be restored by the boys before the squire or conscience catches them.
45325-harper-s-young-people-april-12-188:
One weekly number of Harper's Young People fills this file: volume two, number 76, dated Tuesday, April 12, 1881, price four cents. Its lead piece asks the question every boy asks himself: how shall I make a living? The answer comes first and plainly: by learning some useful trade.

Benjamin Franklin's walk into Philadelphia serves as the great example. The young printer arrived tired and weak with a few pence, bought three penny rolls, and carried the spare ones under his arm past his future wife. Nearly all the good men who succeeded began so, the essay argues. The issue mixes such counsel with pictures and stories, Harper's formula for the young: improve the reader while entertaining the child.
45329-harper-s-young-people-april-19-188:
Harper's Young People was a drawn weekly for the young at four cents. Volume two, number seventy-seven is dated April 19, 1881. One year cost one dollar and a half paid in front then. Toby Tyler, by James Otis, runs on in this number's heart. That tale was begun in number fifty-eight of December last.

Ten weeks with a circus is Toby's lot in the long tale. Part nineteen tells of Mr Stubbs's tricks and his sad end. Toby finds he is lost in the woods in this week's page. Fear strikes him as it would a man full grown there. He sits on a log and counts time by his wee pencil sums.
45337-harper-s-young-people-april-26-188:
Harper's Young People was an illustrated weekly for boys and girls from Harper and Brothers of New York. This number, volume two, number seventy-eight, is dated Tuesday, April 26, 1881. It cost four cents, or a dollar and a half a year. The cover picture shows shad-fishing on the Hudson River.

The lead story, How the Seine Net Was Broken, is by J O Davidson. Three boys, Ralph, Joe, and Scott, meet in a lane and head for the shore. Fishermen in oil-skin suits are hauling a great seine net for shad. Sailing smacks dot the bright water of the Tappan Sea. The tale mixes boy adventure with a working look at the spring shad fishery. Stories, pictures, and short pieces filled each weekly number.
45345-harper-s-young-people-may-3-1881-a:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, May 3, 1881, is one issue of an illustrated weekly for children. Harper and Brothers published it in New York at four cents a copy. This is volume two, number seventy nine, and a picture of gathering mayflowers heads the number.

A May-Day story for girls by Kate Upson Clark leads the issue. Pidgie Mullen begs her tired mother to go on with a tale she half knows. Her sister Belle, an invalid on a lounge, joins in the telling. The mother works hard for her fatherless brood, the tale notes. Other tales, verse, and pictures fill the weekly. Readers get a tender sample of a loved children's paper.
45556-pappina-the-little-wanderer-a-stor:
Katherine Wallace Davis wrote this children's story of southern Italy, Pappina the Little Wanderer, published at Chicago in 1908. Pappina Pierno, seven years old, lives in San Lucia, the Naples quarter where clothes hang forever out to dry. Her family is a tribe too large to count. Unlike her neighbors, Pappina loves to be clean, and delights in combing her silky black hair while other children let theirs go.

Chapters take her to a feste day at Naples, the valley of Pompeii, and Cava. Hardships at Salerno follow, then a reconciliation, adventures along the coast and at Amalfi, and Sorrento, where hardships end. A final chapter promises Naples and a new life. Davis wrote it to teach American children about Italian street children, with warmth and a little pity.
45573-out-with-garibaldi-a-story-of-the-:
Out with Garibaldi, a story of the liberation of Italy, is one of the historical tales for boys written by G A Henty. The front matter of this text is the publisher's list of Henty's tales, with their prices. That list runs to dozens of volumes, each tied to a war or a turning point in history.

The list shows the range of the series: Egypt, Carthage, Jerusalem, King Alfred, the Norman Conquest, Wallace and Bruce, Cortez in Mexico, Clive in India, and Wolfe in Canada. Garibaldi's fight to free and unite Italy takes its place in that line. Henty's tales pair a boy hero with a great campaign, and teach history through march, siege, and battle.
45899-studies-of-travel-italy:
Freeman, the Norman Conquest historian, gathered these studies of travel in Italy for Putnam in 1893. A line of Vergil heads the title page, towns piled by hand on rocks. Arezzo opens the book: the city of Maecenas, with no signs of being frequented by travellers, where a man can hardly get an Italian newspaper. Its clean streets and air, Freeman suggests, nourished the genius of its citizens.

Cortona, Perugia, and the Volumnian tomb follow, with Prae-Franciscan Assisi and Spello. Veii, Fidenae, and Ostia bring the antiquities. A journey to Brundisium makes the second half: Anagni, Ferentino, Alatri, and a church by the camp of Hannibal. Benevento and the Norman buildings in Apulia close at Bari. Freeman travelled with a historian's eye for walls and constitutions, and Italy was a document to be read town by town, never a picture to be admired.
46092-a-little-pilgrimage-in-italy:
Olave M Potter, author of The Colour of Rome, wrote this Italian travel book, first published in 1911 and reissued cheaply in 1913. Yoshio Markino made the eight colored plates and other pictures. A view of Perugia looking toward Assisi stands near the front.

Potter invites the reader away from the great cities, where feet bruise on stone and brick walls shut out the sky. She promises hills, valleys, and towered cities riding on crests. Siena, who belongs to the Madonna, and Perugia, a torch into the valleys of romance, are her stars. The book is a gentle pilgrimage among the little cities of great memories in Italy.
46155-the-fantastic-clan-the-cactus-fami:
The Fantastic Clan, published in 1932, is a study of the cactus family. Its authors are John James Thornber and Frances Bonker. Thornber taught botany at the University of Arizona. The two had written desert books together before. Here they treat all the most important groups of cacti. They aim at sound science, told with the spell of the desert kept in it. The great cactus country, they note, is the American desert of the Southwest.

Paintings, photographs, and pen drawings fill the book. A Mexican night-blooming cereus stands on the frontispiece. The authors thank a long list of collectors and desert scientists for specimens and help. Dedications honor a father who sought the odd and beautiful in nature. They also honor an aunt who collected rare plants. The book is a field guide, a picture book, and a love letter to the desert in one.
46680-fishing-with-the-fly:
Fishing with the Fly is an anthology of fly fishing essays edited by Charles F Orvis and others, published in 1883. Orvis, the Vermont tackle maker, gathered angling writers of his day. The book opens with mottoes from Pope and from Izaac Walton, the patron saint of anglers.

Charles Hallock leads off with Etchings on a Salmon Stream. Hallock doubts that anything new can be written of the salmon, then finds the subject perennially fresh. Propagation, migration, form, and flavour have all been treated before, he concedes. Yet each recurring spring renews the fish's piquancy for the angler. The essays that follow mix instruction with campfire literature. Orvis's volume helped fix the canon of American fly fishing writing while his firm sold the tackle to practise it.
46744-the-camp-of-refuge-a-tale-of-the-c:
The Camp of Refuge is a tale of the conquest of the Isle of Ely, here in a second annotated edition edited by Samuel Miller of Wisbech, with maps. A generation had passed since the tale first appeared, and Miller, a historian of the Fenland, added notes and an appendix rather than rewrite the old story.

The camp of refuge was the Isle of Ely in the Norman Conquest, where Hereward and his men held the fens against William's armies. Miller's preface says his aim is not to make the tale real history but to help young readers, and those with few books, toward the many sources on the subject. The tale mixes legend and record in the old romantic manner.
47177-the-sunbonnet-babies-in-italy:
Eulalie Osgood Grover wrote The Sunbonnet Babies in Italy, published by Rand McNally in 1922. Bertha Corbett Melcher, who created the sunbonnet babies' look, illustrated it with James McCracken. Molly and May, the two little girls in great bonnets, are the guides.

A verse at the front calls Italy a far-away land of sun in a blue sea, with birds singing and flowers springing all year. Molly and May travel there to share its song and play. Grover built a whole shelf of such travel primers, taking her babies to Holland and her Overall Boys to Switzerland. Simple sentences and big pictures teach geography to children just learning to read.
47523-the-bishop-s-apron-a-study-in-the-:
William Somerset Maugham published The Bishop's Apron in London in 1906, calling it a study in the origins of a great family. Maugham had made his name with Liza of Lambeth and Mrs Craddock. This novel, reworked from an early play, starts his long run of cool, observant fiction.

A butler named Ponsonby opens the book, imposing in his sombre garb, while the narrator remarks that the world takes people at their own estimate. Behind such servants stands the family whose rise the novel traces toward a bishop's household. Maugham watches ambition dress itself as respectability, a theme he would work for sixty years. The prose is already dry, exact, and quietly amused.
47656-harper-s-young-people-may-10-1881-:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, May 10, 1881, is an illustrated weekly for the young. Harper and Brothers issued it in New York at four cents a copy, or a dollar and a half a year. This is number eighty of the second volume.

A drawing by Howard Pyle, of Paul Revere at Lexington, heads the number. The lead piece is Hours With the Octogenarians, by Benson Lossing. Thirty or forty years back, Lossing writes, he went on pilgrimage to places hallowed by the Revolution. Living witnesses still held the tales then, though age was taking them fast. He kept their narratives in notes for the youth of a later day. The first tale is the Fifer of Lexington. At Concord in October 1848 he met Major Barrett, hale at eighty-seven, whose wife saw the British scamper in 1775.
47669-harper-s-young-people-may-17-1881-:
Harper and Brothers published Harper's Young People as an illustrated weekly for boys and girls. This number is dated Tuesday, May 17, 1881, in volume two, and sold for four cents.

Alden's serial, The Cruise of the Ghost, leads the issue. Charley and his friends haul their boat ashore and spend two weeks lengthening her. They lead every rope aft so the helmsman need not leave his post. Charley builds a carriage for a small cannon and lashes it before the mast. Naming her proves the hardest task of all. Tom offers America or George Washington, and Harry floats Red Revenger. Joe's word Ghost wins, for the boat is white as one.
47672-harper-s-young-people-may-24-1881-:
Harper's Young People was an illustrated weekly magazine for boys and girls, sold for four cents a copy. This issue, number 82 of volume two, is dated Tuesday, May 24, 1881. The Harpers of New York published it, and a year's subscription cost a dollar and a half.

The lead story, by Lizzie Champney, tells of the Colosseum in the days of the Emperor Caracalla. A young Christian student walks the great arena and thinks of the martyrs who died there. The rest of the weekly mixes stories, facts, puzzles, and pictures in the usual Harper style. It shows what bright American children were given to read on a spring week in 1881.
47684-harper-s-young-people-may-31-1881-:
Harper's Young People, volume two number 83, published by Harper and Brothers at New York on Tuesday, May 31, 1881, cost four cents, or a dollar fifty a year in advance. The lead story, Two Kinds of Courage, opens with Old Slack Limestone on the tavern steps at Dicksonville, a master of tobacco-chewing and story-telling. Slack, a turf-layer by specialty, is laying the boys' lawn-tennis ground while Horatio coaxes out the story of little hunchbacked Philip.

Slack speaks, the narrator says, the purest Yankee, a language by itself. He corrects the boys twice: Philip's broken back came neither from the war nor the sea, but from an act of duty at Milliken's Mill. The dialect tale contrasts Slack's lazy philosophy with the grit he praises in Philip. The weekly mixed fiction and pictures for young readers.
47699-harper-s-young-people-june-7-1881-:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, June 7, 1881, is one issue of Harper's illustrated weekly for children. It is volume two, number 84, priced at four cents, or a dollar and a half a year. The issue opens with an engraving called The Defeat of the River Pirates. Below it begins chapter five of a serial, The Cruise of the Ghost, by Alden, author of The Moral Pirates.

The cruise had begun in the issue of May 10. In this chapter the boy sailors listen in darkness to the sound of oars. Their own vessel lies hidden, and an invisible row-boat is moving near them in the cold mist. They expect attack by thieves at any moment and whisper for orders. Charley, their captain, says that if the men come, they must fight. To lose the boat would mean starving in the marshes.
47709-harper-s-young-people-june-14-1881:
Harper's Young People, volume two, number eighty-five, is an illustrated weekly dated Tuesday, 14 June 1881. Harper and Brothers of New York sold it at four cents a copy. Its lead piece, On Wheels, is by the Captain. It tells of the bicycle meet held in Boston on Decoration Day that year.

Boston boys saw two processions that day: the military parade with its wagon-loads of flowers, and a line of bicyclers a mile and a half long. Eight hundred wheelmen of the League of American Wheelmen rode in double file, with silken flags for the clubs and bugles sounding. Boys brought up the rear under an expert rider and made a creditable show. The article warns boys who fear a fall: such boys will never learn, and no cowards are wanted among the wheelmen.
47729-harper-s-young-people-june-21-1881:
Harper Young People, volume two, number eighty six, for Tuesday, June twenty first, eighteen eighty one, cost four cents. Harper and Brothers in New York published the illustrated weekly. A lead story, The Fair Messenger by Benson J Lossing, opens the number with a plate of the arrest of Emily Geiger. Lossing tells the tale as a traveller. He was at Orangeburg, South Carolina, in January eighteen forty nine.

His purpose was to visit the battle ground of Eutaw Springs on the Santee River, he says. He hired a horse and gig and travelled thirty miles by sunset. He lodged at a planter house near Vance Ferry. A venerable woman of eighty four, Mrs Buxton, told him of the Revolution on the Upper Santee. She knew Marion, Sumter, and Horry as a maiden of seventeen, she said. Young readers get history, tales, and pictures weekly.
47732-harper-s-young-people-june-28-1881:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, June 28, 1881, volume two, number eighty seven, cost four cents. A comic poem by Margaret Eytinge leads the issue. Dear Me tells of a dead grasshopper in a garden. A sparrow mourns him, then buries him in her own way, to a cabbage rose's laughter. The joke lands soft, in the paper's gentle house style.

Next comes George Stephenson and the railroad, a science piece for young readers. Trains in England, it marvels, run at seventy miles an hour. That is as fast as a balloon or a storm wind. Yet rail reached such speed only in the last forty years. The engine, small and low, holds a giant's strength. The weekly mixed verse, invention, and tales so a child took in the modern world without noticing the lesson.
47763-the-cornish-coast-south-and-the-is:
The Cornish Coast (South) and the Isles of Scilly is a topographical volume by Charles Harper. The front matter lists Harper's road books: the Portsmouth, Dover, Bath, Exeter, and Great North roads among them. He wrote the annals of England's old highways in volume after volume. Here he turns from the road to the shore.

The same method serves him: travel the ground, gather its stories, and draw the places. The south Cornish coast and the Scilly Isles give him harbours, wrecks, smugglers, and saints in plenty. His other books in the list, on the Tower of London and the smugglers, show his taste for the picturesque past. The volume is a companion for the traveller who wants history with his sea air, told in Harper's full, anecdotal manner.
47926-harper-s-young-people-july-5-1881-:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, July 5, 1881, is number 88 of volume two of the illustrated weekly for children. Harper and Brothers sold it at four cents a copy, or a dollar fifty a year. The lead article, Canoes and Canoeing, is signed Nautilus. Drawings by Davidson show the annual regatta of the New York Canoe Club in the Upper Bay.

The piece explains the racing canoes, none over fifteen feet long, and their huge balance-lug sails. Ballast bags of shot weigh as much as the boat itself. A comic upset race capsizes every canoe at a signal. Canoes cost from twenty to one hundred dollars, and a national meeting at Lake George is announced.
48272-harper-s-young-people-july-12-1881:
Harper's Young People was the Harper weekly for the young, four cents a copy and a dollar and a half a year. This number is the eighty-ninth, dated Tuesday, July 12, 1881. A picture of the dunce's seat leads it. David Ker opens with A Palace Under the Sea, a trip to the Orkney, Shetland, and Faroe islands.

For a month's holiday, Ker says, few places beat those northern islands, though the rough sea plays sad tricks on a poor sailor. Great black cliffs rise two or three hundred feet from the water, with thousands of sea birds screaming around them. Wide gray moorlands without a tree spread behind. The weekly mixed travel, tales, and pictures in the Harper way.
48289-harper-s-young-people-july-19-1881:
Harper's Young People for July 19, 1881, is one weekly number of an illustrated paper for youth. Harper and Brothers of New York issued it at four cents, or a dollar and a half a year in advance. It is Number 90 of Volume Two. A bold plate opens the number.

The plate shows Flora Macdonald urging sailors to keep up a fight. Benson Lossing's article tells her story in North Carolina. It goes back to 1745, when Prince Charles Edward landed in Scotland to claim the British crown. Beaten, he hid as a fugitive in the Hebrides. Flora, a young Scotch woman fresh from school in Edinburgh, helped him escape to France. Lossing follows her later life across the Atlantic. The number mixes history, pictures, and story in the house style of Harper's.
48324-harper-s-young-people-july-26-1881:
Harper's Young People, volume two, number ninety-one, is an illustrated weekly dated Tuesday, July 26, 1881. Harper and Brothers of New York sold it for four cents. A picture of Richard Whittington heads the number. The opening poem, The Little Millionaire, lets a small daughter whisper her riches to her father.

Her wealth is pennies, nickels, quarters, and one piece of gold from an uncle's letter. Her father sighs that she is ten thousand times richer than he. A prose piece then tells of Dick Whittington as the model merchant of the middle ages, part romance and part real history. Stories, poems, and pictures fill a paper made to be read aloud in the family circle.
48597-harper-s-young-people-august-2-188:
Harper Young People, volume two, number 92, for Tuesday, August 2, 1881, is one issue of the Harper illustrated weekly for the young. Harper and Brothers printed it in New York at four cents a copy. A serial tale, Tim and Tip, by James Otis, opens the number.

A plate shows Tim bearing the marks of Captain Babbige whip. Chapter one, Tim Flight, opens with a strayed notice read aloud from a country newspaper. The notice offers a reward for a runaway boy of about eleven years, with short light hair, a turned up nose, and a very tanned face. When last seen he wore a suit of faded blue clothes and had with him a yellow dog, long in body and short in legs and tail. Young readers of 1881 got a runaway serial in weekly parts.
48610-harper-s-young-people-august-9-188:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, 9 August 1881 forms this number of a weekly sheet for the young. It is the ninety-third number of its second year. The price is four cents a copy, or a sum and a half for a year paid in front. Cuts fill the sheet from its first page. The first piece is a poem in the tongue of the day, Picnic Sam, by Will Carleton.

The poem calls the young to crowd round and hear of Sam. He lived in a tall block of let rooms, up a great count of stairs. His room was what room he could squeeze into when he came off the worn streets. He lived high, in the jest of the poem, yet never had the gout. For the most part he took his meals out of doors.
48803-harper-s-young-people-august-16-18:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, August 16, 1881, is number 94 of the weekly's second volume. Harper and Brothers sold it in New York for four cents. A picture after a painting by Greuze, captioned simply "Unhappy," leads the issue.

The first story, How a Buoy Saved the Boys, is by Matthew White. Sam Finney rises an hour early and hurries to the steamboat dock at Fair Farms. The steamer Laura Pearl is bringing his city friend Tom Van Daunton and a new rowboat. The two boys row, crab, fish, and fall overboard all summer long. Other tales, pictures, and puzzles fill the number, in the mix that made the paper a staple of American childhood.
48889-the-catholic-world-vol-14-october-:
Catholic World, volume fourteen, is a half year of a monthly magazine. The Catholic Publication House of New York issued it in eighteen seventy two. The volume runs from October eighteen seventy one to March eighteen seventy two. Its contents mix essays, tales, reviews, and science for Catholic readers.

Christianity and Positivism opens the volume, then Egyptian civilisation follows. Authority in matters of faith and Catholicity and Pantheism fill long pages. The Dollinger scandal, the martyrs of Arcueil, and the International are treated. Clarke Lives of the American Catholic Bishops is reviewed in its pages. Craven Fleurange runs as serial fiction through the half year set.
49029-harper-s-young-people-august-23-18:
Harper's Young People was an illustrated weekly for boys and girls, and this issue, dated Tuesday, August 23, 1881, cost four cents. Its lead story, The Mistake About Hamp See by George Cary Eggleston, opens in a village post-office where neighbors wait for the mail. Old Riley Vaughn defends young Hamp against the schoolmaster, who says the boy cannot grasp the Latin verb yet takes to arithmetic by instinct.

The exchange, told in rich country speech, argues that a grip on ideas matters more than a grip on words and rules. Around the story, the weekly offered its young readers pictures, tales, and facts in the Harper house style. The issue preserves both a lively defense of practical sense over book learning and a sample of what American children were given to read in the early 1880s.
49046-harper-s-young-people-august-30-18:
Harper Young People, volume two, number 96, for Tuesday, August 30, 1881, is one issue of the Harper illustrated weekly for the young. Harper and Brothers printed it in New York at four cents a copy, or one dollar and fifty cents a year in advance.

The issue opens with a poem, The Old Gun, on a cannon that hurled bolts of thunder in battle and now sleeps in the sun. Children frolic round it, noisy with innocent glee, above the graves of the slain on that long ago plain. George Cooper poem Compensation follows, trading each green leaf for a golden one and each parching beam for a drop of rain. A mother kiss answers every passing care. A piece on ancient travelers begins the prose. Young readers of 1881 got poems, tales, and pictures in one weekly sheet.
49138-harper-s-young-people-september-6-:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for boys and girls, sold for four cents by Harper and Brothers of New York. This issue, number 97 of volume two, is dated Tuesday, September 6, 1881. Its front picture shows a small passenger with a large valise.

The lead serial is Tim and Tip, the adventures of a boy and a dog, by James Otis, in its sixth chapter. Tim has left old Mose's kitchen and watches the bustle of a steamer sailing: deck hands, newsboys, and fruit sellers. A very small boy struggles aboard with a valise several sizes too large, which knocks his legs at every step. The scene sets a new acquaintance for Tim.
49360-harper-s-young-people-october-4-18:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for boys and girls, sold for four cents by Harper and Brothers of New York. This issue, number 101 of volume two, is dated Tuesday, October 4, 1881. A year's subscription cost a dollar and a half in advance.

The issue opens with The Talking Leaves, an Indian story by William O Stoddard. Two girls, Rita and Ni-ha-be, watch from a mountain pass as men below crowd around something found in the grass. Ni-ha-be's sharp eyes pick out her father and Red Wolf in the valley. The tale begins a serial in the lively mix of story, verse, and fact that the paper gave its young readers each week.
49392-harper-s-young-people-october-11-1:
Harper's Young People for October eleventh, eighteen eighty one, is an issue of an illustrated weekly for young readers. Published in New York by Harper and Brothers, it sold for four cents. The issue is number one hundred two of volume two. A picture of Isaac Newton at the age of twelve heads its first article, Newton's Childhood.

Newton is called the greatest of modern philosophers and mechanics in that opening. He was born on Christmas Day sixteen forty two, three months after his father's death, it tells. So small and feeble was he that none thought he would live a day. The weak infant grew to eighty four, and his boyhood machines open a life of invention for young readers.
49537-the-spider-and-the-fly: Charles Garvice's The Spider and the Fly was sold by Street & Smith of New York as number 300 of the Eagle Series, at ten cents. The opening pages kept here give that series list, running back through hundreds of cheap tales, Garvice's own among them: For Her Only, My Lady Pride, and Love's Dilemma. No page of the novel itself stands in these leaves, so its plot cannot be told from them. The book's shape is plain: a ten-cent love tale in a long line of them.
49587-harper-s-young-people-october-18-1:
Harper's Young People, number 103, is dated October 18, 1881. The illustrated weekly cost four cents from Harper at New York. A year ran to a dollar and a half. The Story of the Negro Fort leads this number's pages. Eggleston wrote that story for the young readers of the weekly.

In the late war the Spanish governor allowed a base. Pensacola served the British from Florida soil. Jackson invaded Florida in retaliation on his own responsibility. An eccentric Irish colonel enlisted Seminole Indians there, it tells. In 1815 he made an astonishing treaty with those Indians. Britain was bound to fight whenever they chose war. We had made peace with Britain months before that treaty, it notes. The British government refused to ratify the treaty in the end. Eggleston gives young America a fort, a colonel, and a powder blast.
49719-harper-s-young-people-october-25-1:
Harper's Young People of October 25, 1881 is an issue of an illustrated weekly magazine for the young, published by Harper and Brothers in New York. The issue is volume two, number 104. It sold for four cents, or a dollar fifty a year in advance.

The opening story is Vic Whitney's Revenge, by George Cary Eggleton. A bully named Hen Little knocks down a smaller schoolmate and tears his clothes. The victim warns that he will repay the blow even if it takes ten years. The boys vote to shut the bully out of their games. Stories, pictures, and departments for young readers fill the rest of the number. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
49777-harper-s-young-people-1881-index-a:
Harper's Young People for 1881 survives here as its index volume. Harper and Brothers issued the weekly at New York. Copyright was entered in 1881. The index to illustrations runs in alphabetical order. Each entry gives a short title and a page number. Abdullah and his Friends stands at page 296. An alligator upsetting a canoe stands at page 68. Mice playing base-ball close the run at page 784. Aunt Ruth's Temptation is listed in parts, with scenes from the tale.

Boats get their own head, with plans of a catamaran and a row-boat. Birds, bears, and boot-blacks fill the B entries. The index maps a year of stories, pictures, and pastimes for young readers. It shows the range of a leading American children's weekly in the early eighteen eighties.
49846-florizel-s-folly:
Florizel's Folly is a book of past lore by John Ashton. It was put out at London in eighteen ninety nine. Three teen plates stand in the book. The front plate shows a famed maid of the tale. Ashton's past books treat cheap tale books and old jest prints.

The book tells the rise of Brighton. The town grows from an old coast port to a gay resort. Its first parts treat French raids on that coast. They treat a king's flight to France from its shore. Then a great duke takes a hand in the young prince's life. The maid of the plate is the prince's wife in all but law. The prince bore in jest the name of a swain in a famed play.
49862-harper-s-young-people-november-1-1:
Harper's Young People of the first of the eleventh month of eighteen eighty one is one week's print of a sheet for the young. It is count one hundred and five of its third year. Its price is four cents a copy. Its year price is set at the head of the page. The rights of the print are held by the house of Harper.

The front plate shows a great catch of a boy, drawn by a named hand. The lead tale is of the strange lot of Ben Buttles, by Frank Converse. Each boy knows the lure of the rod, the tale starts. That lure holds if he gets no more than bites of the small fly kind. It is the hope of what one may catch that lifts the sport.
49886-harper-s-young-people-november-8-1:
Harper's Young People was an illustrated weekly for boys and girls, sold at four cents. This number, volume three, number 106, is dated Tuesday, November 8, 1881. Harper and Brothers published it in New York. A bold plate called Killing the Panther fronts the issue.

The lead serial is The Talking Leaves, an Indian story by William Stoddard. Chapter six finds Steve Harrison and his friend Murray on a ledge of gold ore. Murray feels the old gold fever burn again at the touch of nuggets. He tells Steve how Apaches left ruins that took his wife and child. Steve hopes the gold may pull him from life among the Lipans. The chapter mixes frontier grief with the lure of sudden wealth.
50013-harper-s-young-people-november-15-:
Harper's Young People for November 15, 1881 is one issue of a children's weekly. Harper and Brothers of New York put the paper out each Tuesday. The issue stands as volume three, number 107 of the young folk's sheet. Four cents bought a copy, a dollar fifty the year in advance. A picture called Washing Dolly stands near the front of the number.

A verse called Farewell opens the issue with beasts and birds speaking. The honey-bee, the fly, the cricket, and the squirrel take their turns. The thrush sings that nothing is left to sing but farewell now. A tale called Luck follows, about Charlie Foster and his school prize. Boys called each win of his just like his luck, it seems. The story asks whether luck or work makes a boy's rise in life. Tales, verses, and pictures fill the rest of the weekly number.
50085-harper-s-young-people-november-22-:
Harper's Young People for November 22, 1881, is an illustrated weekly for the young. Harper and Brothers made it at New York, at four cents a copy or a dollar and a half a year. This is volume three, number one hundred and eight. A front plate shows the way the little folks keep Thanksgiving. Margaret Sangster leads with Elsie's Thanksgiving, a poem told to a doll. The doll came with an auntie from Paris, far over the wide blue sea.

Elsie explains the feast as her grandma taught her, late in the fall. Nuts and apples are in, field work is done, and thanks go to the Father above. Cousins crowd the table at home, and dance and play end the day. The issue gives verse, tales, and pictures for a family week in 1881.
50100-how-to-do-chemical-tricks-containi:
How to Do Chemical Tricks, by A Anderson, promises over one hundred experiments for the parlour and the stage. Frank Tousey published the booklet in New York, with a copyright of 1898, in his series of cheap manuals for boys. An opening lesson sorts matter into elements and compounds before the tricks begin.

The tricks themselves run to coloured flames, strange inks, gases, and changes that seem like magic but rest on simple reactions. Each is set out as a recipe the reader can follow with common chemicals. Books of this kind sold science as entertainment: a boy who worked through them learned the names and habits of common substances while showing off wonders to his friends. The plain directions and low price put the little laboratory within reach of almost any reader.
50163-harper-s-young-people-november-29-:
Harper's Young People, volume three, number 109, is the issue dated Tuesday, November 29, 1881. Harper and Brothers sold it in New York for four cents.
