A year's run cost a dollar and a half in advance. The lead tale is How Tom Primrose Protected His Father, by Sydney Dayre. A front plate shows boys shouting that others are getting away.

Mr Primrose comes home worn out from a trial thirty miles off. He prosecuted two noted criminals and fears the jury may free them. A letter from a sheriff then gives fresh hope of holding them on a bank robbery charge. His wife fears revenge from such men. The tale builds family warmth and legal peril for young readers of the weekly.
50396-harper-s-young-people-december-6-1:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, December 6, 1881, volume three, number one hundred ten, cost four cents. A picture headed A Friend in Need is a Friend Indeed fronts the issue. Its lead tale is Max Rander's Adventure in Berlin, by Matthew White. Max tells how he and his brother Thad, lately moved to Berlin, were let loose to walk the great avenue Unter den Linden by themselves.

The boys watch for Emperor William's carriage, but Max always drags Thad round a corner when it comes, fearing shots at the Kaiser. Max has grown deeply wary of the Germans and their odd ways, he admits, and still gets into a dreadful mix within a week. A crowd at a large building, looking for all the world like a circus, draws the boys in. The weekly mixed such tales with pictures and facts for its young American readers.
50502-harper-s-young-people-december-13-:
Harper's Young People was an illustrated weekly magazine for children, priced at four cents. This number, 111 of the third volume, is dated Tuesday, December 13, 1881. A subscription cost a dollar and a half a year. The cover story is Lady Rags, by Margaret Eytinge, and it opens in the thick of a snowball war.

The Woods and the Tins, gangs from two streets, have fought for more than a year. Their war began over a parrot that one boy borrowed and kept all vacation. The Tins charge the snow covered building site while the Woods defend their cellar fort, Fort Hurrah. Captives are dragged inside in triumph. The Christmas setting, the battle, and the girl at the story's heart made lively weekly reading for the magazine's young audience.
50545-harper-s-young-people-december-20-:
Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for boys and girls, reached its Christmas number on Tuesday, December twentieth, eighteen eighty-one. Harper and Brothers sold it at four cents, a dollar fifty a year. A notice warns that the serial story and post-office box stand omitted from the Christmas number. They will resume next week, it promises.

Shamruck, or the Christmas Panniers, by Frank R Stockton, leads the holiday pages. There was once a gloomy old giant named Shamruck, Stockton begins. His castle stood on a hill not far from a great city of the King. Shamruck was not dangerous, and no one feared him, the tale says. He simply never cared to do anyone the slightest service. At Christmas he grew more melancholy and more alone.
50809-harper-s-young-people-december-27-:
Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for children, closes its year with the issue of Tuesday, December 27, 1881. Harper and Brothers sold it at New York for four cents a copy.

A Christmas poem leads the number. It sings of the angel voice on Judah's plain. Then comes a story by Mrs Frank McCarthy. Young Harry shoots a crow off a wood-pile, thinking it a fine target. The bird is Jo's pet, blind in one eye and ragged. Jo clasps the dead crow to his chest and sobs. Harry, a lad of twelve, owns his fault at once. He vows to find a nicer pet. The weekly mixed poems, tales, and pictures for the nursery trade. Its tone here is tender, with a plain lesson on care for the weak.
51544-the-state-its-history-and-developm:
Franz Oppenheimer wrote The State, its history and development viewed sociologically, in an authorised translation by John Gitterman, copyrighted in 1914 and reprinted by the Vanguard Press in the nineteen twenties. Oppenheimer was a Berlin doctor who gave up medicine for economics, lecturing at Berlin from 1909 and holding a chair of sociology at Frankfurt from 1919. His libertarian views made him enemies in high places.

Oppenheimer argues that the state began in conquest, when victors settled on the beaten and lived off their labour, and that its forms still carry that birthmark. The book became a classic of libertarian and sociological thought, read far beyond Germany.
51723-harper-s-young-people-january-3-18:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, January 3, 1882, volume three, number 114, is an illustrated weekly for the young from Harper and Brothers of New York. It costs four cents; a year in advance is a dollar fifty. A frontispiece shows New-Year's Dinner in the Nursery. It opens with verse, A Child's Puzzles, by Mrs Margaret Sangster.

Her poem asks where the old years go when their work is done. Are they tucked away to sleep out of sight of the sun, or shut into crystal jars behind the stars. The child wishes mother a happy New Year, and wishes she had kept awake till twelve. A story follows, Max Rander on a Bicycle, by Matthew White: the family leaves Germany in October for an English village near a town where bicycles are made. Within a week the mania to ride one seizes the boy.
51948-henry-is-twenty-a-further-episodic:
Samuel Merwin wrote Henry Is Twenty, a further tale of Henry Calverly the third. Collins issued the book in London in nineteen hundred twenty one. The tale had run month by month in a magazine first. Kind letters from readers greet the book in its front note.

Henry is no hero of the neat pattern tale, Merwin owns at once. His vanity, self love, and quick soft spots stand too plain for that. A touch of genius in him knots each of his young trials. Martha, Corinne, and Mamie Wilcox share his split young heart. A neat tale would bar such a split love, Merwin laughs. Henry slays no town dragon in Sunbury that gay summer. Uncle Arthur’s worldly wise words fall on a deaf young ear. At forty he may do well; at twenty, no, says his maker.
52077-corinne-or-italy:
Madame de Staël wrote this novel, Corinne, or Italy, here in Isabel Hill's English translation, published at London by Bentley in 1833, with the odes turned into English verse by Landon. The catalog title is a line of Petrarch the book quotes: you will hear the fair land that the Apennines divide and the sea and Alps surround. The translator's preface warns of her task: French holds several meanings in one word, and repetition, an elegance in French, is a barbarism in English.

Corinne is a poetess of genius, crowned at the Capitol in Rome, and the novel is half love story, half a tour of Italy's art and ruins. It made Italy romantic for a century of readers. De Staël wrote it in exile from Napoleon. The book is her country of the mind.
52318-harper-s-young-people-january-10-1:
Harper’s Young People for Tuesday, January 10, 1882 is number 115 of its third volume. Harper and Brothers published the illustrated weekly at New York. It cost four cents a copy, or a dollar and a half a year in advance. The Holidays Over heads the number as its opening theme.

Marjorie’s New Year’s Eve, by Mrs Lillie, carries the fiction of the issue. Marjorie hunts for a particular door in a castle of crystals in that tale. At last the key turns in the lock, and she goes in frightened and trembling. A large room covered with crystals opens before her there. A gallery on one wall overlooks some other room beyond. The weekly served boys and girls with tales, puzzles, and pictures.
52553-harper-s-young-people-january-17-1:
Harper's Young People, volume 3, number 116, was dated Tuesday, January 17, 1882, in New York. The illustrated weekly cost four cents, or a dollar fifty a year in advance. A front picture shows a large handsome sleigh drawn by four coal-black horses passing like a flash. The lead tale, Just for Fun, is by Matthew White.

White tells of Percy Vance, a new boy at grammar school whose age no one can guess. Girls think him past fifteen for his height, while boys, seeing his slim frame and timid grey eyes, say not over ten. He cannot tell a marble from a top but tops his classes, to the envy of fun-loving Dan Tregwin. Snow and sledding soon change the game.
52630-harper-s-young-people-january-24-1:
Harpers Young People for January the twenty fourth is one issue of a weekly for youth. The Harper house in New York put the paper out at four cents a copy. This issue is number one hundred and seventeen of its third year. The date on its head is the year eighteen eighty two.

A winter poem by Sarah Jewett leads the issue with a boy on a sled. Prints and tales for boys and girls fill the rest of its pages. A front print shows a boy head by a famed French painter of old. The paper sold by the year for a dollar and a half in advance. Short verse, sport, and home fun mark the tone of the whole weekly.
52773-harper-s-young-people-january-31-1:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, the thirty first of January 1882, is number 118 of volume three of Harper and Brothers' illustrated weekly for children. The New York weekly cost four cents a number, or a dollar fifty a year in advance.

The issue opens with a picture called The Little Sleepers and a story by Emily Huntington Miller, The Longest Day in the Year. Her hero Dan insists it is the longest day, whatever the almanac says. Dan knows the foggy morning is bad weather for haying and tip-top for fishing, and he means to fish. At breakfast his father orders the scythes put in order for the lower meadow tomorrow, and warns Dan not to need hunting after. Dan's appetite vanishes: he hates the heavy, creaking grindstone, and he knows his father will keep him waiting all morning.
53102-the-lonely:
The Lonely is a short tale of first contact by Judith Merril. It first ran in a science fiction magazine in October of nineteen sixty three. Art for the tale was drawn by an artist named Lutjens. The story takes the form of coded notes sent between star posts.

A scholar on Pluto sends a trimmed script of a picked up show to a friend. The show seems to be a lecture set beamed from near the core of the galaxy. Its beam moves far faster than light and talks of Earth men in plain terms. Codes and notes cloak the find as a top secret file for two men. The tale asks what such far watchers would make of the human race.
53166-dick-and-dolly:
Carolyn Wells wrote this children's book, with copyright in 1909, about nine-year-old twins named Dick and Dolly. The twins have spent most of their years with Grandma Banks and an aunt. Chapter titles promise a brook, gardens, a playground, a secret, and a gay party. Ada Budell drew the pictures for the book.

Wells was known for her Marjorie and Patty series for young readers. Here the twins meet new friends, pay calls, and get into mild scrapes and treats. An auction sale, a playhouse, and a coronation add fun along the way. The story is light and warm, made for children who liked tales of home and play.
53187-harper-s-young-people-february-7-1:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for boys and girls, and this number came out on Tuesday, February 7, 1882. Harper and Brothers sold it for four cents a copy, or a dollar and a half a year. It is number 119 of the paper's third volume.

The lead story is Art's Organ Adventure, by Matthew White. The Dickson family is spending the winter in Paris, and Art, who is fourteen, means to see the whole city. He has done the galleries, churches, prisons, and palaces with his family. Now his mother and sister are lost in dressmaking, and his father reads American papers for hours. Art slips away on his own. Weeklies like this one filled the week for young readers, with stories, pictures, and facts in every number.
53205-letters-from-switzerland-and-trave:
Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy are travel writings by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, in English dress. Morrison translated the works for this edition, published by George Bell and Sons in London in 1881. They first appeared in English as part of the Autobiography of Goethe, Truth and Poetry. This volume is the second volume of that autobiography set.

The Swiss letters record a young poet journeys among the Alps with friends of his Weimar circle. The Italian travels record the famous journey that remade Goethe as an artist in his own account. In Italy he studied art, antiquities, plants, and the life of the streets as a student again. English readers of the Victorian age met the German classic largely through such volumes. This one joins the two great travel records of his life between the same covers for them.
53297-harper-s-young-people-february-14-:
Harper's Young People, volume 3, number 120, was dated Tuesday, February 14, 1882, in New York. The illustrated weekly cost four cents a copy. A front picture notes that no one had a larger supply of valentines than Theodora and Bessie. The lead tale, A Valentine and a Mission, is by Margaret Eytinge.

Eytinge tells of Electa Eliza, twelve years old and lame, who is never seen without the baby. Since the child was three weeks old she has cared for him all day but Sunday, while her widowed mother washes and irons. The baby is round-eyed, red-cheeked, and bald, so wise at times he seems a jolly old dwarf in disguise. School, once her joy, is lost to duty.
54468-harper-s-young-people-february-21-:
Harpers Young People for a week in the winter of the early eighteen eighties is a pictured weekly for the young, priced at four cents. It came out each Tuesday from a great New York house. A years run cost a sum set on its front page, paid in advance.

Its front plate shows a scene from a tale of a day of love notes. That tale stands at a late part in the copy at hand. A boy on a ladder hears voices and must clutch his perch to keep from a fall. A man of ill fame has come back for a fell deed, the boy grasps. A hoard lies hid by a fire place, in a locked nook below the floor. Fear shakes him as he weighs a move.
54513-harper-s-young-people-february-28-:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for the young, and this issue is number 122 of volume 3, dated Tuesday, February 28, 1882. It sold for four cents, or a dollar and a half a year in advance. A poem, The Little Frost Queen, leads the number, with a print to match.

Her cheeks are rosy in the frosty air and her heart is gay with the bright day. Next, a grandson tells of Charley Otis's ride, a tale from his grandfather's boyhood. Tales, verse, and prints fill the rest. Young readers of 1882 got a fresh pack each week, and this one keeps its charm.
54538-miss-esperance-and-mr-wycherly:
Allen Harker wrote Miss Esperance and Mr Wycherly, a novel published at New York in September 1908 by Charles Scribner's Sons. The catalog title keeps the second name with a stray mark. Harker also wrote A Romance of the Nursery and Concerning Paul and Fiammetta.

The first chapter introduces them, and the second brings the coming of the children. Chapters follow the education of Mr Wycherly, the secretiveness of Mause, and a girl named Robina. The awakening of Mr Wycherly and a rechristening by young Edmund show who teaches whom. Cupid abroad and a Sabbath chapter soften the schoolroom comedy. Harker writes of children invading a bachelor's ordered life, a favorite Edwardian theme. The book is gentle, funny, and fond of its small invaders.
54625-harper-s-young-people-march-7-1882:
Harper and Brothers published this number of Harper's Young People on Tuesday, March 7, 1882. It is volume three, number 123 of the illustrated weekly. The price was four cents, or a dollar fifty a year in advance.

Raja's tale Father Time's Dilemma leads the issue. There is a commotion in the moon. Father Time has rheumatism in both legs and cannot leave his fireside seat. For thousands of years he has never failed to visit the earth. Now he is helpless, and a day's neglect may end the world. His wife picks up his fallen scythe and steadies the hour-glass while his children weep.
54979-the-yellow-holly:
Fergus Hume wrote The Yellow Holly, for Dillingham at New York, rights held in 1903. Hume was the author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. This edition was issued on October 1, 1908, the front pages say. A front plate shows a crisis: Lola pulls a packet from her breast. She runs with it to the fire to burn the papers.

George shoots past her and snatches them out before they catch alight. He thrusts the packet into his own pocket in the plate. Contents open as a hostess receives, then give Brendon's story. A nine-days' wonder, a lovers' meeting, and what a Mr Ireland knew follow. The red man, a bacchante, and clever Mrs Ward fill the middle. A woman scorned, a trump card, and a recognition lead toward the truth. Hume spins society mystery in his practiced hand.
56122-harper-s-young-people-march-14-188:
Harper's Young People, the illustrated weekly for boys and girls, reached number 124 on Tuesday, March 14, 1882. Harper and Brothers sold it for four cents, or a dollar and a half a year in advance. Each number mixed stories, poems, and pictures for the schoolroom and the fireside.

The lead story is Polly Gardner and the Draw-Bridge, by Julia Hildreth. Polly is spending her vacation with Aunt Mary in the country. She would be perfectly happy, the tale begins, but her father and mother had to stay in the city. Five weeks without them feels like five months. She sits on the horse block kicking one foot, watching her aunt drive off to visit a sick neighbor, while bees hum and willows stir. A picture called Teasing Tom stands at the head of the number.
5643-ranson-s-folly:
Richard Harding Davis wrote Ranson's Folly and Others, a story collection illustrated by Frederic Remington, Walter Appleton Clark, Howard Chandler Christy, E. M. Ashe, and F. Dorr Steele. Contents include the title story, The Bar Sinister, A Derelict, La Lettre d'Amour, and In the Fog. The opening illustration shows Ranson facing a door, spinning a revolver around his fourth finger while a voice commands him to throw up his hands.

Davis writes adventure with a newspaperman's pace, from western gunplay to love letters and fog-bound suspense. Readers get five brisk, well-illustrated tales by a famous war correspondent and storyteller.
56629-harper-s-young-people-march-28-188:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for the young from Harper and Brothers of New York, and this issue is number 126, dated Tuesday, March 28, 1882. The price was four cents, or a dollar and a half a year. Art cuts head the pages, as the sub title brags.

The lead tale, Doing Something by Ada Carleton, opens on a poor house by a creek. A boy called Merry sits at a bare table with one roast potato, a dish of salt, and a bit of bread for the whole stock of food. Rent is a full quarter in arrears, and the landlord Colley has begun to frown. Merry vows to earn, and to bring his mother the biggest half of his dinner.
56677-harper-s-young-people-april-4-1882:
Harper Young People for April 4, 1882, is a weekly issue for the young. Harper and Brothers sold it at New York for four cents a copy. Volume three, number one hundred twenty seven, leads with a serial tale. Mister Stubbs Brother, by James Otis, opens the number in chapter one.

Toby Tyler, back from running away with a circus, faces a new scheme. Reddy Grant urges him to help start a boys circus of their own. Toby knows circus life too well and mourns his dead monkey still. A year has softened his refusal, and school is out for summer now. A trip to Bob Atwood house opens the amateur circus plot.
56717-members-of-the-family:
Members of the Family is a set of western tales by Owen Wister, printed by Macmillan at New York in 1911, with pictures by Dunn. The eight stories first ran in magazines between 1901 and 1911. Scipio Le Moyne, a cowhand from Wister's earlier books, leads off the set.

In Happy-Teeth, Scipio lies bound in bandages after a wild horse throws him at Stinking Water. His mates think him done for, but he vows he will not die for years. Spit-Cat Creek, Timberline, and The Gift Horse follow. One tale stars a drake with means of his own. Readers get dry humour, rough country, and cowhands drawn with real affection.
56741-harper-s-young-people-april-11-188:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, April 11, 1882, is volume three, number 128 of the illustrated weekly for the young. Harper and Brothers of New York sold it at four cents a copy, or a dollar fifty a year in advance. An Easter poem by S S Conant leads the number, under a plate crying, for lo, he hath arisen.

The verses tell of the darkened sun, the rent veil, and the sad disciples who thought their master's reign had ended. The Marys go at break of day with ointment and spices, and find an angel in shining white. The poem ends with the call to seek him in Galilee and weep no more. The weekly mixes verse, tales, and pictures for the parlour table.
56771-harper-s-young-people-april-18-188:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for boys and girls from Harper and Brothers of New York, sold for four cents a copy. This number, dated April 18, 1882, leads with a tale by James Otis, famed for Toby Tyler. A fine cut shows men training an old blind horse.

Otis's serial, Mr Stubbs's Brother, finds Bob and his pals hard at work on a boy circus. They build a saddle, pick acts, and plan a show at three cents a head. Small Abner Bolton, a boy on crutches, comes near and draws Bob's wrath. The mix of serial tales, cuts, and facts made the paper a weekly treat. It shows what keen young readers in 1882 held in their hands.
56840-harper-s-young-people-april-25-188:
Harper's Young People for April 25, 1882, is one number of Harper's illustrated weekly for children. It is volume three, number 130, priced at four cents or a dollar and a half a year. The lead serial is Mister Stubbs's Brother, by James Otis, author of Toby Tyler, begun in number 127. Chapter four, The Pony, continues the boys' circus scheme.

Chandler Merrill has willingly consented to let the boys use his pony. He did so with the kindly prophecy that the little animal would kick their brains out if they were not careful. Bob has brought the pony along, to prove he told the truth and to keep the consent from being withdrawn. The pony stands gazing suspiciously at the Douglass horse, ragged-coated where it has rubbed off in spots. A passage preserved in the copy gives Bob's excuse for the pony's temper.
5727-the-tale-of-freddie-firefly:
The Tale of Freddie Firefly follows a small firefly through a woodland summer of dances, plans, and parades. Chapters trace a merry dancer, a fine plan, getting ready at a stone wall, banners, and a torchlight parade, before schemes, songs, thistles, and an escape test Freddie's promise. Each short chapter offers one clear scene for a young listener.

Children meet insect neighbors with distinct tempers, from peppery Polly to Jennie Junebug, and they learn how keeping a promise matters when plans go wrong. The story is gentle, musical, and easy to read aloud, with adventure kept small enough for bedtime. It suits early readers who enjoy animal tales where courage means helping friends and finishing what was begun.
57308-the-mute-stones-speak-the-story-of:
Paul MacKendrick wrote The Mute Stones Speak, the story of archaeology in Italy, published in New York in 1960. MacKendrick walks the reader through what diggers have found, age by age. The first chapter covers the earliest Italy of stone-age sites, earthwork villages, and the great stone towers of Sardinia.

Later chapters take up the Etruscans, early Rome and its kings, and Roman colonies such as Ostia. Whole sections follow the building of Augustus, the odd finds tied to Tiberius and Nero, and the towns buried by Vesuvius, above all Pompeii. The plan is to let stones, walls, and graves tell the story that written records miss. MacKendrick wrote for general readers, and the book became a standard first guide to the field in Italy.
57494-trolley-folly:
Henry Wallace Phillips wrote a set of tales printed in Indianapolis in 1909. Phillips was known for Red Saunders. The title tale gives the book its name. Its hero Jimmie Horgan works a trolley car and has a first taste of fortune in a fine lawyer office of mahogany and glass.

Jimmie is famed for his soft hand on the brake. Riders who would not seem quick have made fine jumps to catch his car, the tale jokes. Other tales tell of a coin expert, a mascot of a ball team, a small canoe, and ten minutes that feel like forever. Camp life, crime, and peace making round out a book of light, warm tales.
57692-harper-s-young-people-may-2-1882-a:
Harper and Brothers published this weekly for young people at New York for four cents. Volume three, number 131, is dated Tuesday, May 2, 1882, at $1.50 a year in advance. A picture shows one by one the lights flaring up, at the head of a lighthouse tale.

Peters tells of Huldah Deane's heroism in that opening story of the number. A gray sea tosses beneath barren rocks where a tall lighthouse stands, the tale begins. Huldah gazes wistfully at the dreary picture and envies an osprey its freedom, wishing herself anywhere but the rock where nothing happens, until a wreck gives her the heroism of the title.
57796-harper-s-young-people-may-9-1882-a:
Harper's Young People is an illustrated weekly magazine issue dated May 9, 1882. Harper and Brothers published it in New York at four cents. It is volume three, number one hundred thirty two. A year's subscription cost one dollar fifty in advance. The issue opens with a serial story, Mr Stubbs's Brother. James Otis, author of Toby Tyler, wrote that serial. This instalment is chapter six, called Old Ben. It began in number one hundred twenty seven of the weekly.

Toby watches anxiously as each circus wagon comes up in the chapter. He fails to recognize any of the drivers at first. Then the well remembered monkey wagon appears in the distance. Old Ben drives it in a sleepy sort of way. Toby runs to meet the team with his friends streaming after him. The weekly mixed serials, pictures, and fun for children.
57842-harper-s-young-people-may-16-1882-:
Harper Young People of May sixteenth, eighteen eighty two, is a week sheet for youth. Year three, sheet one hundred thirty three, is the mark on its leaf. The Harper house of New York sold it at four cents a copy. A front cut shows a cat at a music drill with a grave face. The lead tale is The Scarlet Glow by Percy Earl of that staff.

Fletcher, age ten, and Amy, age eight, stay at a Swiss lake inn. Their widowed sire leaves them for a day trip to the high hills. A ban on boats is his last word as the coach bears him off. Talk of hill views and wild blooms lures Amy to beg a climb. Fletcher wavers, torn between the ban sense and pride in his charge.
57887-harper-s-young-people-may-23-1882-:
Harper's Young People, the illustrated weekly for boys and girls, reached number 134 of its third volume on Tuesday, May 23, 1882, price four cents. A picture shows Uncle Daniel receiving his guests. The serial in progress is a Toby Tyler story by James Otis, begun in number 127, here at its dinner party chapter.

The scene is a sideshow's private exhibition, given as a mark of respect to Toby. Treat gives the signal for the snake charmer to begin, and the doors will open to the public in fifteen minutes. The boys are not anxious to leave, and Toby goes to find Ella while his friend stays safe with the skeleton's party. The weekly mixed serials, science, and sport for the nursery and schoolroom.
57968-harper-s-young-people-may-30-1882-:
Harper's Young People for May 30, 1882 is one weekly issue of an illustrated paper for the young, issued at New York. It is volume three, number one hundred thirty five, priced at four cents. The lead story is The Big Blast at the Stone Quarry, by William Stoddard. A picture head shows a dog with the caption Bow Wow.

Stoddard's tale opens on a Friday afternoon in May, at the door of an academy in a place called Prome Centre. Boys and girls pour out squad by squad, the story says. One boy, Felix McCue, must wait later than the rest. His teacher takes a warm interest in him, but he would rather hear it at any time but after school. His slate carries a big message for his waiting friends.
58023-harper-s-young-people-june-6-1882-:
Harper's Young People, number 136 of volume three, dates to Tuesday, June 6, 1882. Harper and Brothers sold the illustrated weekly at New York for four cents.

A tale by Mrs John Lillie leads the number. Mary Grey, seventeen, calls her brothers Ben and Lewis in softly. A dear little brother waits upstairs to see them. Ben is nine and Lewis six. The baby lies in a pink and white cradle in a sunny room. He has a black head, blinking eyes, and doubled pink fists. A dimple sits in one cheek. The boys' fear of being put out of power melts at the sight. He gets his pet name, Scrap, on the spot, though christened Philip. The weekly fed children tales, verse, and pictures.
58110-harper-s-young-people-june-13-1882:
Harper and Brothers issued this number of Harper's Young People, their illustrated weekly for the young, on June 13, 1882. It cost four cents, or a dollar and a half a year in advance. The number leads with a hunting tale by Edward Stevenson, Captain Banner's Lynx.

Captain Banner, of the Yellowbird Ranch in California, eats his luncheon on a hot rock while his three mongrel dogs watch a ravine. A lynx is below, and the dogs will soon hold it at bay, as the picture promises. Around the tale, the weekly mixed stories, facts, and pictures for its young subscribers. Readers get a Tuesday in the life of an 1882 schoolboy.
58223-harper-s-young-people-june-20-1882:
One weekly number of Harper's Young People, volume three, number 138, dated Tuesday, June 20, 1882, sold for four cents, or a dollar fifty a year. A serial called Mr Stubbs's Brother, begun in number 127, leads the issue. Its author, James Otis, had written Toby Tyler. Chapter twelve is a rehearsal. Toby tells Uncle Daniel of plans for the long delayed circus.

Abner is to ride up to the pasture to watch all that goes on. The old gentleman shakes his head doubtfully, fearing for the invalid boy. A picture shows Toby and Abner attending the rehearsal. Harper's weekly mixed serials, pictures, and instruction for young readers.
58357-harper-s-young-people-june-27-1882:
Harper and Brothers published this weekly for young people at New York for four cents. Volume three, number 139, is dated Tuesday, June 27, 1882, at $1.50 a year in advance. A picture shows men unrolling a schooner's sails at the head of this summer number.

James Otis's serial of the circus reaches chapter thirteen in these pages. The results of long training is that chapter's title in the serial's running head. Stubbs's brother, the monkey, watches Ben begin to revolve as an acrobat, then leaps from his tree and catches the whirling boy by one leg, in Toby Tyler's show world.
58448-harper-s-young-people-july-4-1882-:
Harper's Young People for the fourth of July 1882 is one number of an illustrated weekly for the young, put out by Harper and Brothers of New York. It is volume three, number one hundred and forty. The price was four cents a copy, or a dollar and a half a year. The front page leads with a tale called Through the Tunnel, by Edward Stevenson. Its first scene has Dr Flaxman in his chaise before the Petry house in Wicketiquok village.

Young Cadmus Petry comes round the house at last. His father has gone up to Lafayette by the early train, and his mother with him. The doctor is vexed: he has a letter that turns his whole view of a land deal. The boy's father means to buy part of a farm that day, on the doctor's own advice.
58457-harper-s-young-people-july-11-1882:
Harper's Young People was a weekly paper for boys and girls, sold by Harper and Brothers of New York for four cents a copy. The issue dated Tuesday, July 11, 1882, is number 141 of its third volume. A year's subscription cost a dollar and a half, paid in advance.

The issue leads with chapter fifteen of Mr. Stubbs's Brother, a serial story by James Otis. In this part, Toby and his friends at a small circus try to catch a loose monkey that is tearing the tent while the crowd laughs and cheers. Serial tales, pictures, and short pieces filled each number. The issue gives a clear sample of what American children read for fun in the early 1880s.
58552-harper-s-young-people-july-18-1882:
Harper Young People was a weekly paper with plates, made for the young by Harper and Brothers in New York. The copy here is book three, part 142, dated Tuesday, July 18, 1882. A single copy cost four cents, and a year cost a dollar and a half in advance. The first page opens with a long rhymed piece.

That piece tells of two girls, Maud and the teller, at the farm of their grandpa. Their best task is to watch a flock of white sheep all a long day. The lambs know their names and crowd close when called. At dusk the girls feed them salt and think of the Good Shepherd. The verse links farm play, mild faith, and care for weak things. Such a sheet mixed song, tales, and facts for boys and girls each week.
58654-the-psycho-analytic-study-of-the-f:
Flügel wrote a study of the family that uses the new mind science of his day. The book came out in London in 1921. Flügel taught at University College in London. He also held a post in the world group for this field. Two short quotes at the start set the theme. One is from Plato and one is from Samuel Butler.

Inside, the book asks how deep, half-hidden thoughts shape home life. It looks at love, hate, and bonds between parents and young ones. It treats dreams and slips as clues to those bonds. Readers get an early view of how this school read the home.
58832-harper-s-young-people-july-25-1882:
Harper's Young People for July 25, 1882, is a weekly number of Harper's illustrated paper for youth. It is Volume Three, Number 143, priced at four cents. The lead article, by Helen Conant, tells of Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia. A plate shows the saint.

On a beautiful hill near Eisenach in Germany stands an ancient castle, the Wartburg. There, in 1521, Martin Luther found shelter after the Diet of Worms. He spent a peaceful year translating the Bible in a room still preserved with its table and book-case. The castle, among the oldest in North Germany, rose in the eleventh century. Legend says its first builders carried soil in baskets up the hill to make a building ground. Conant joins the saint's story to the castle's long fame for young readers.
58896-harper-s-young-people-august-1-188:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, August 1, 1882, an illustrated weekly priced at four cents, leads with chapter 18 of Mr Stubbs's Brother. The serial is by James Otis, the author of Toby Tyler. The boys of the circus have their hands full with the monkey of the title. They pull porcupine quills out of him and march him home between Joe and Toby. Then they debate chaining him in the tent as a wild man of Borneo. A picture of Bob and the grizzly bear fills the front page.

Harper and Brothers built the paper for the families that took their monthly, with serials, pictures, and short pieces in every number. This issue preserves the serial in mid-course, the way its first readers met it: one chapter a week, with the show going on until the next Tuesday.
59103-harper-s-young-people-august-8-188:
Harper and Brothers published this weekly for young people at New York for four cents. Volume three, number 145, is dated Tuesday, August 8, 1882, at $1.50 a year in advance. A picture shows Toby rescuing a crowing hen from the brother of Stubbs, in James Otis's serial.

That serial, 'Mr. Stubbs's Brother,' reaches chapter nineteen in this number. The breaking up of the show is the chapter's title in the contents note. The boys find cages ready-made and talk of Abner over Aunt Olive's frying doughnuts, until the dainties go up on a high shelf, in the circus tale begun in number 127.
59126-faulkner-s-folly:
Faulkner Folly is a crime tale by Carolyn Wells, out from a Doran house in nineteen seventeen. Beatrice Faulkner halts on the great stair of her house in the first scene. A foot man peers through a door left a crack wide in the hall. The house was the dream home of the man of craft who first held it. Its cast is the grand sort called Colonial in the land of the tale.

Wide steps, low lifts, and great square rests made that stair his pride. Part names trace the case through talk, tale, and Mrs Faulkner word. Gem stones, shut notes, and a sight dream fill the mid part names. A plea of not there, a call for proof, and a jail catch come late. A stair scene and a quiz of asks and tells close the scheme.
59410-harper-s-young-people-august-15-18:
Harper’s Young People for August fifteenth, eighteen hundred eighty two, is volume three, number one hundred forty six. Harper and Brothers sold the weekly for four cents. W L Alden leads with The Cruise of the Canoe Club. Alden had written The Moral Pirates and a cruise of the Ghost.

Four boys want four canoes at seventy five dollars each. Their whole purse holds seven dollars and thirteen cents. Uncle John has given them boats in the past and merits mercy now. They may sell their sail boat Ghost to raise part of the sum. A lost brig they once found holds rich South American timber. Her salvor may gain ten thousand dollars for the haul. The boys go down to Burling Slip to see her once more.
59523-harper-s-young-people-august-22-18:
One weekly number of Harper's Young People fills this file: volume three, number 147, dated Tuesday, August 22, 1882, price four cents. The issue opens with a history of Egypt for young readers, by Eugene Lawrence. Egypt, he begins, is the most interesting of countries because it is probably the oldest.

We borrow nearly all our arts and sciences from the Egyptians, Lawrence argues, from the alphabet onward. Moses studied in Egypt, and its glass-makers, goldsmiths, and builders taught the western nations. Harper's magazine wrapped such lessons in stories, pictures, and puzzles for the parlor table. A summer number shows the formula: solid improvement, brightly lit, for boys and girls who were expected to know things.
59557-harper-s-young-people-august-29-18:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, August 29, 1882 (volume three, number 148) sold for four cents, or $1.50 a year, from Harper and Brothers of New York. The number's serial is The Cruise of the Canoe Club, begun two numbers earlier and written by Alden, author of The Moral Pirates. Chapter three finds Charley standing in four feet of water beside his sunken canoe, the Midnight, a mile from shore.

Charley will not desert his boat, and he sets Harry, Joe, and Tom to work raising her. The boys pass painters from the Sunshine, the Twilight, and the Dawn, duck under water to reeve lines through the stern-post, and heave together. The scene is told in the easy, practical talk of boys who know canoes, and it carries the serial's charm of camp and water adventure.
59586-harper-s-young-people-september-5-:
Harper's Young People for September 5, 1882, is an illustrated weekly issue. Harper and Brothers published it in New York at four cents. Volume three, number 149, it sold at a dollar fifty a year. A picture called Too Hot, drawn by Jessie Shepherd, fronts the issue. A poem, The Burial of the Old Flag by Mary Barr, leads.

Barr sings of Newcastle upon Tyne as a town of proud record. Roman eagles, Saxon, Dane, and Scot left glamour on that fair spot. Monarchs of every line from William Rufus had grace for loyal Newcastle. Pageants by the Nuns' Gate and up Pilgrim Street fill her verse. One May morn in 1763 a sight thrilled that town of the north.
59639-harper-s-young-people-october-3-18:
Harper's Young People for October 3, 1882, is an issue of an illustrated weekly for children. Harper and Brothers published it at New York for four cents. A year's subscription cost a dollar and a half in advance. The issue is volume three, number 153. Its lead story, The Soldier's Cheese, is by David Ker. The scene opens at the village of Andermatt at daybreak in 1799.

All night the villagers have packed and fled into the northern passes. At dawn the St. Gothard slope turns black with troops. Russian grenadiers, Cossacks, gunners, and hussars pour down the mountain. The imperial standard of Russia flutters above them. The deserted village pleases the soldiers, who have not eaten for two days. The tale grows from that hungry army's arrival. Stories and pictures for young readers fill the rest of the number.
59644-harper-s-young-people-october-10-1:
Harper's Young People for Tuesday, October 10, 1882, leads with A Very New Cow, a story by William O Stoddard. Katy Chittenden meets the family buggy at the gate with news. All the Chittenden cows are in Mr Gates's pasture. The deacon groans that it is all the new cow's doings. The costly, brindled creature kicks the milk pail three feet and is held in awe by the household. The boys who drove the herd up get a defense from the deacon himself.

The number costs four cents and belongs to the paper's third volume. Harper's built the weekly on serials, pictures, and farm stories like this one. After dinner the deacon and William take axe, maul, and nails to fix the fence. The tale settles into its comedy of a troublesome cow.
59649-harper-s-young-people-october-17-1:
Harper and Brothers published this weekly for young people at New York for four cents a copy. Volume three, number 155, is dated Tuesday, October 17, 1882, at $1.50 a year in advance. A picture shows a boat under way for Coney Island at the front of the number.

James Otis, author of 'Toby Tyler,' supplies a story in three chapters called 'Their Girl.' Chapter three opens on the bright morning of a famous excursion in his tale. Johnny and Jimmy, up before light, dress with painful care for the boat that leaves the pier at ten, in a number full of stories and pictures.
59660-harper-s-young-people-october-24-1:
Harper's Young People for October twenty fourth, eighteen eighty two, is a single issue of an illustrated weekly for young readers. Published in New York by Harper and Brothers, it sold for four cents a copy. The issue is number one hundred fifty six of volume three. A story called Carbo opens the number.

That story starts on a raw night at a small western rail junction, with a narrator waiting for an express train. Verse, tales, pictures, and short pieces fill a children's paper of this kind. The price, yearly rate, and copyright line are all printed on the first page. The issue shows what respectable family reading for the young looked like in that era.
59666-harper-s-young-people-october-31-1:
Harper's Young People was Harper and Brothers' illustrated weekly for boys and girls, and this is number 157, dated Tuesday, October 31, 1882, priced at four cents. The number leads with Nan, a serial by Lillie, whose heroine Nan Rolf is thirteen and living in shabby rooms above her step-aunt's cheese and butter store in Bromfield. Her cousins Marian and Philip share the dingy parlor, where Nan groans over her arithmetic on a rainy day.

The weekly mixed serial stories, pictures, and short pieces for the young, at a price a child could carry. Nan's story promises the usual riches of the form: a refined heroine in vulgar surroundings, family secrets, and slow betterment. Bound volumes of the paper raised a generation of American readers before the boys' and girls' magazines took over.
59668-harper-s-young-people-1882-index-a:
Harpers Young People 1882 Index is the year list book of that drawn week sheet for the young. It came out at New York in eighteen eighty-two. It lists the plates of the year in the order of the word book. First heads run from a call to board a train to halls of kin of old, each with its page. Beast heads list a famed show mans tents in the cold half and a tale of beasts.

Heads past that treat babes, bags, air craft, and bears with their pages. A shore town, a ball game at a famed ground, and a bath room stand in the rows. Bird heads list past a score of plates, from swal in their nests to hum birds. The list lets a young hand find a past plate or tale of the year by its head word.
60445-jim-and-wally:
Mary Grant Bruce wrote Jim and Wally, a tale of war and Ireland for the young. Ward, Lock and Company issued it in London in nineteen hundred seventeen. Bruce had won her crowd with the Billabong books of Australia. War, the first chapter, drowns the reader in Flanders mud at once.

Duckboards sink and vanish under the tramp of fresh troops there. Shell holes and wire scar the strip of No Man’s Land ahead. Cast off rifles, spiked helms, and lost caps dot that dead ground. Bold Flemish sparrows hop and chirp where no man dares stand. Yellow envelopes, those dread War Office notes, head the next act. When the Boys Come Home stands third in the tale’s bright list. Then Ireland calls: Donegal, brown trout, and Lough Anoor await. A cave among rocks and a fight in the dawn close the book.
60495-miss-billy:
Miss Billy, a neighbourhood story by Edith Keeley Stokely and Marian Kent Hurd, is a novel of a small street and its people. Lothrop published it in Boston in April 1905, with pictures by Charles Copeland.

The first chapter shows number twelve Cherry Street, a wretched, woebegone house whose windows drip with dew from moss-grown eaves. A poem about the house opens the chapter before spring slips in with paint and a scrubbing brush. Chapters follow ways and means, new neighbours, a load of dirt, and next door doings. Trials, a broken sidewalk, and weeds give way to a child garden and a lawn social. A Hallowe'en chapter and a story of Horatius break up the street scenes. Margaret lends assistance before fair skies close the tale.
60554-harper-s-young-people-november-7-1:
Harper and Brothers published this weekly for young people at New York for four cents. Volume four, number 158, is dated Tuesday, November 7, 1882, at $1.50 a year in advance. A picture shows all hands scrambling up the rigging, at the head of a sea story in the number.

James Payn tells of peril and privation in the wreck of the Juno there. Women sufferers from shipwrecks are the most to be pitied, Payn argues at the start. Bremner, the captain's wife, bound from Rangoon to Madras, had as terrible an experience as ever fell to her sex, with a Lascar crew and one mate to tell it.
60596-harper-s-young-people-november-14-:
Harper's Young People was an illustrated weekly for children, and this issue is dated Tuesday, November 14, 1882. It cost four cents, or a dollar fifty a year. The first piece is a poem called Waiting, by Margaret Johnson, about a child told by every grown-up to be patient.

The child waits for summer, a wax doll, a rose blossom, and growing tall, and at last decides that waiting does no good. A tale of adventure in the Suez Canal follows, set as trouble brews in Cairo under Arabi Bey. More stories, pictures, and fun fill the number in the weekly's usual mix. It is a bright sample of the reading served to American children in 1882.
61347-socialism-and-the-family:
Socialism and the Family gathers two papers by Wells on the socialist creed. Fifield of London brought the small book out in the year 1906. The first paper was read to the Fabian Society in October 1906. The second had appeared first in the Independent Review journal. Together they state modern socialism's attitude to family life pretty completely.

The first paper bore the title Socialism and the Middle Classes then. Wells sets out three things to keep distinct in the argument. Socialism itself is a large conception of a sane, organized state. The socialist movement stands as a second, separate thing to weigh. The middle classes make the third term of his whole inquiry. Wells counts himself one witness in a growing multitude of them. Generations must toil and testify, he holds, and the count matters little. His tales, from the Time Machine to Kipps, fill the front list.
61481-silence-is-deadly:
Bertrand Shurtleff wrote this naval science fiction tale for Astounding Science-Fiction in April 1942. Its opening note argues that radio is a basic need in modern naval work. Silence all radio, the note warns, and that kind of silence would be deadly.

Commander Bob Curtis wakes from a doze aboard the cruiser Comerford as knuckles hammer at his cabin door. Nelson, his navigating officer, always knocks in a hurried rat-a-tat. With Curtis sits Zukor Androka, an elderly Czech scientist and a guest of the United States navy. The calm opening sets up a wartime plot built on signals and their loss.
61499-monopoly:
Vic Phillips and Scott Roberts wrote a science fiction story for Astounding Science-Fiction, where it ran in April 1942. Their opening note warns that skill and good management can grow a monopoly, and that a tyrant will try to wield it as a weapon. The scene is Venus City, a new settlement where one great firm runs much of daily life.

Brian Hanson heads the Venus Consolidated Research Organization and takes fierce pride in the city he helped build. His lab chases vitamin counts while his staff beg him to rest. From that proud, tireless start, the tale asks what happens when one man's drive meets a company town with no rival. Power, work, and control form the knot the plot must cut.
62342-stonehenge-and-other-british-stone:
Norman Lockyer, the astronomer, wrote Stonehenge and Other British Stone Monuments Astronomically Considered, the phrase the catalog keeps as its subtitle title. Lockyer founded the study of the heavens as a tool for dating ancient buildings. His list of works runs from a primer of astronomy to studies of the sun.

Lockyer argues that Stonehenge and like monuments were built to mark the sun's and stars' rising at set seasons. By measuring their alignments he tries to fix the dates when they were raised. The book draws stone circles into the science of the sky. Critics have argued over his dates ever since. The work still stands as the bold start of a new field, the astronomy of ancient sites.
62484-ruffled-doilies-and-the-pansy-doil:
Ruffled Doilies and the Pansy Doily is Star Book number 59, a ten-cent crochet pattern booklet from the American Thread Company, copyrighted in 1948. Its cover promises doilies to set off treasured bric-a-brac, frame a rose, or give a table a cool snowflake look.

The first pattern, Double Ruffle number 5901, is shown on the front cover. It takes four balls of the company's Star mercerized crochet cotton, size 30, at two hundred and fifty yards each, and a steel hook number 12. From a chained ring the rows build outward in double crochet and chain spaces, reaching knot stitches by the ninth row. The finished centre measures thirteen and a quarter inches before the ruffle. Sister booklets on edgings, rugs, afghans, babies, potholders, and tablecloths are listed at the back, ten cents each.
6409-how-to-speak-and-write-correctly:
Joseph Devlin, edited by Theodore Waters, writes a 1910 guide to speaking and writing correctly, from the Christian Herald Bible House. Requirements of speech open it, with vocabulary, parts of speech, and requisites. Essentials of grammar, the sentence, figurative language, and punctuation follow, with letter writing, errors, and pitfalls to avoid.

Style, suggestions, slang, newspaper writing, and choice of words carry the second half, with small words given their importance. Devlin notes that language has changed since old complex sentences ruled, and that terseness, brevity, and clearness are now the aim. Punctuation has simplified with that change. The book is a working manual, plain and direct, for readers who want plain, correct English.
64117-the-christmas-holly:
Marion Harland wrote The Christmas Holly, published in New York by Sheldon and Company in 1867. Harland opens with a salutary: a memory of a Christmas Eve walk taken many years before. Young, unreasonable, and rebellious, she had walked alone into the country under low, steel-gray heavens. A few snowflakes fell through the biting air.

The scene she recalls is bleak: sterile hills, leafless woods, and a tame ice pond dug for summer use. Inside, she felt a dull, icy calm and distrust of her fellows. The tale grows from that mood, as Christmas pieces of her age often did. Harland, a famed writer on home life, turns a holiday walk into a lesson on faith and temper.
650-pictures-from-italy:
Charles Dickens sketches Italy from a traveler's eye in this volume, printed with American Notes in the 1913 Chapman and Hall edition. The Reader's Passport opens the tour, followed by Lyons, the Rhone, Avignon, Genoa, Parma, Bologna, Verona, Milan, Rome, and a Rapid Diorama. Eight illustrations by Marcus Stone show peasants, catacombs, and street folk.

Dickens writes with vivid, personal prose, refusing grave examinations of government in favor of what he saw and felt. His Italy is streets, inns, and faces, not guidebook facts. The book endures as a lively travel sketch, where a novelist's eye turns a journey into a story.
65046-the-british-campaign-in-france-and:
The British Campaign in France and Flanders, January to July 1918, by Arthur Conan Doyle, is the fifth volume of his history of the Great War. Hodder and Stoughton issued it in 1919. A front list shows the earlier volumes marching year by year from Mons and the Marne through the Somme and Passchendaele.

This volume opens with Russia's collapse freeing German armies for the west, then follows the great March offensive against the Third and Fifth Armies. Doyle names divisions and regiments as they stand or break. Written just after the events, it is earnest patriotic history from the creator of Sherlock Holmes.
66288-the-fifty-fourth-of-july:
The Fifty-fourth of July is a science fiction story by Alan E. Nourse, first printed in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in March 1954. Nourse was a doctor who wrote science fiction on the side. His tale is set in New Mexico, near a crashed ship that local men guard and fear.

Matt Matthews comes back to camp at night to find a city stranger who wants to be taken down to the ship. The ship stands for a past crash that wrecked the local economy, and Matt feels bound to destroy it. Yet destroying it may also destroy the future. The story is a tense short piece about fear, pride, and hard choices after disaster.
67739-the-evolution-of-marriage-and-of-t:
The Evolution of Marriage and of the Family is a work of the lore of man by Letourneau. He was the chief clerk of the lore band of Paris and a chair man in its school. The book stands in a set of lore books run by Havelock Ellis. It was put out at London in eighteen ninety one. Its list of parts is a full map of its theme.

The first part treats the root of wed life in the world of beasts. The true place of man in that world, breed, and love in beasts fill it. The next treats wed life and the home past beasts. Young rear and the home in beasts stand in its heads. Then comes the hard doubt of a first stage of free love past all men.
69064-the-little-acrobat-a-story-of-ital:
Janie Prichard Duggan wrote The Little Acrobat, a story of Italy printed at Boston in 1919 with pictures by Nana French Bickford. Duggan dedicates the book to the memories of two little angelicals of Rome. A frontispiece shows the pale apparition of Natale startling them all, at page 167.

The tale opens along the white road, where men and a sturdy girl of fifteen walk beside the horses in the powdery white dust. Behind the big wagon lags Natale, a slight boy of eight or nine, dusty from the road: a child of an Italian circus family. Nonna, the ring, the festival of San Lorenzo, and a gift for the circus follow, then separation and the caged bird of the fields.
69310-the-wiser-folly:
The Wiser Folly is a novel by Leslie Moore, published by Putnam in New York and London in 1916. The scene is the village of Malford, with its old church, its mural paintings, and its watchful neighbors. A prologue closes the Delancey affair, then the story turns to rumor, a meeting, and a black and white goat. Corin theorizes, Molly Biddulph misbehaves, and an old priest recalls an old-time tragedy.

The book runs to fifty-one chapters, most of them short. Storm, fallen oaks, and long conversations carry the plot toward its miracle. Hutchison drew the frontispiece, a hero calm in voice and wild at heart. Moore writes quiet English village fiction of the Edwardian kind, warm with talk and gentle with judgment.
70291-x-mas-sketches-from-the-dartmouth-:
Edwin Osgood Grover, of the Dartmouth class of 1894, edited X-Mas Sketches from the Dartmouth Literary Monthly, printed at Concord, New Hampshire, in 1893. The little book reprints the tales and pictures of the college magazine's Christmas number. Grover calls it the first volume of a hoped-for series called In Green and White.

Grover is modest about the contents: not masterpieces, he says, but a fair sample of present college fiction. Several stories are their authors' first appearance in print, and the thumb-nail sketches are a first try at college magazine illustration. Contents include Suite Four, Our Winter Birds, A New Year's Legacy, By Proxy, and Christmas Eve at the Club. The volume was meant as a souvenir of the magazine and a spur to story telling among the students.
70765-the-kansas-university-quarterly:
The Kansas University Quarterly is a scholarly journal, and this text is volume one, number four, dated April 1893. The University of Kansas published it at Lawrence for fifty cents a number. The number holds two works: Penology in Kansas, by Blackmar, and a bibliography of municipal government in the United States, by Hodder.

Blackmar opens by praising the state penitentiary at Lansing as one of the best prisons in the far west. The journal's committee of publication lists the university's leading professors. Such quarterlies carried the research of young state universities to the scholarly world. This early number shows the fields Kansas men worked in: prisons, government, and law.
71229-john-s-lily:
John Lily is a novel by Eleanor Price, published at London in 1894 with pictures by Groome. Price had written A Loyal Mind, Alexia, and Red Towers before this tale. Contents open with a little child, storm and sunlight, and home at Markwood. The churchyard stile, a fair, and in the dark carry the early chapters.

Truth, parting, danger, and a stranger mark the turning points in the list of heads. Taken away and given back promise loss and return for the child Lily. Seven years after closes the story with a leap across growing years. A frontispiece shows Lily flushing as she stands looking at John in the scene.
71244-nelly:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote Nelly, a tale for the young put out at Philadelphia in 1867. Its short title calls a good heart the best wealth a child can hold. The American Sunday-School Union sold the book in two towns. A note at the front states the aim of the tale in plain words.

That note says the tale shows the worth of truth and faith in small things and great. Nelly Ryan, a poor girl, leans on the gate of the home of her grandmother. She watches a line of well dressed girls walk past on their way to church. Her tone at first is sharp and full of despair. The tale then tests if hard work and a true heart can lift her. A clerk who can be trusted, the note adds, is worth a high wage.
71712-the-humour-of-italy:
The Humour of Italy is an anthology of Italian comic writing in English translation, published in London in 1892 in the International Humour Series edited by W H Dircks. A Werner selected and translated the pieces and added an introduction, notes, and a biographical index. Fifty-one illustrations by Arturo Faldi accompany the text.

The pieces run from Boccaccio's Calandrino story and Sacchetti's tale of Dante and the smith through Machiavelli, Castiglione, and Ariosto. Cellini offending the Pope, Berni writing to his patron, and stanzas from Tassoni's mock epic The Rape of the Bucket all appear. The book surveys five centuries of Italian wit for English readers who knew the classics mainly by name.
72219-cicely:
Cicely is a story of three years, in three volumes, by Ennis Graham. Graham also wrote She Was Young and He Was Old, the title page notes. The London edition carries a dedication dated December eighteen seventy three. A motto at its head ties love and death to music in the minor key. Contents are given volume by volume.

Volume one heads name a widow's soup and a Mr Guildford of Sothernbay. A second summons and a garden song follow. Volume two moves through work and play, shadows before, and summer days. Volume three opens with a disillusioned head and passes after the ball. Friend and wife closes the list. Chapter one begins with a pastor's little daughter watching a stranger smile in the street.
72372-the-fool-of-the-family:
The Fool of the Family is a story by Bracebridge Hemyng, issued in a series called the Round the World Library. The publisher's opening pages place the book among the tales of Jack Harkaway and his comrades. Readers are told that Jack's adventures in out of the way corners of the globe are classics that all should read.

Jack is praised there as a splendid, manly figure, full of life, strength, and curiosity. His companions include a Professor Mole, who is described as very funny. His enemies, by contrast, are said to be anything but funny. The series list runs through many Harkaway titles, from school days to Oxford and pirates. The Fool of the Family stands as number twenty nine in that line.
72979-introduction-to-sally:
The author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden wrote To Sally, issued in London by Macmillan and Company in nineteen twenty six. Section one opens on Mr Pinner. Mr Pinner was a God fearing man, who was afraid of everything except respectability, it begins. He married Mrs Pinner when they were both twenty. By the time they were both thirty, if he had had to do it again he would not have, it adds.

Mrs Pinner had several drawbacks, the tale lists with dry humour. One was, she quarrelled, and Mr Pinner, who prized peace, was obliged to quarrel too. Another was, she appeared unable to have children, and he was fond of children. Another, while it lasted the worst, was that she was excessively pretty, it says. Sally, a foundling taken in, changes the house. Novel readers get Elizabeth von Arnim wry village tale.
7308-the-history-of-mr-polly:
H. G. Wells's History of Mr Polly opens with its hero on a stile between two threadbare fields. Suffering acutely from indigestion, he cries Hole, then Ole, then a beastly silly wheeze of a hole. Polly lacks introspection, Wells notes, so he projects each afternoon's discomfort onto the world, discovering afresh that life as a whole is beastly.

From that comic stile the novel follows a small shopkeeper's revolt against a dull life, toward freedom, love, and a fresh start. Wells mixes humour with sympathy, letting Polly's odd private idioms carry a serious wish for a better life. The book remains one of his warmest, most humane comic novels.
73165-the-house-of-de-mailly:
Romance at the court of France opens The House of de Mailly, a novel by Margaret Horton Potter issued by Harper and Brothers in 1901. Pictures by Keller go with the story. The book is inscribed to the dearest friends and critics of the author. Its action is split between France and America, in two books named Claude and Deborah.

The first book moves through a gallery of mirrors, the chapel, and Marly. It ends with the farewell of Claude, the hero. The second book brings a ship in, a plantation, and Annapolis into the tale. A governor’s ball and a set of pearls mark its high scenes. Potter weaves old France with colonial Maryland in her plot. The novel belongs to the historical romances that crowded the shelves of its day.
73707-playmate-polly:
Amy E Blanchard wrote Playmate Polly for girls. Hurst and Company issued it at New York in 1909. George W Jacobs held its copyright that year. Blanchard had written Little Miss Oddity before. Little Miss Mouse and Mistress May stand hers. Twelve chapters carry Jessie's tale.

Up Hill and Down opens the book at page nine. Playmate Polly herself enters at chapter two. The Neighbor of the Yellow House comes third. Aunt Betty and A New Pet follow in turn. A Mystery and Taking Pills fill the middle. Dapple Gray and The Gray Kitten come next. Across Water and Who Took the Spoons build late. What Was Found Out closes the tale. Jessie's school road runs Bridge, Railroad, Hill each day. Ezra Limpett waves the red flag at the crossing. Small town girlhood in Blanchard's kind pages turns a school walk into the day's adventure.
7464-the-adventures-of-sally:
P. G. Wodehouse's Sally opens with a party that is plainly a success, though it rallied after an uncertain start. Sally looks down the long table, happy at last, while the patrons of Mrs. Meecher's select boarding house talk and laugh. The talk turns, as it often does, to Sally's legacy and what she should do with it, while her brother Fillmore's white evening waistcoat causes a stir.

Across the table, a mild young man with a deep voice is ready to bet every cent on Benny Whistler for the heavyweight championship. He is convinced that Battling Tuke has been got at and means to lie down. That mix of money, boxing, theatre, and romance drives Sally's adventures on both sides of the Atlantic. It is Wodehouse at his sunniest, with a heroine who keeps her head while everyone around her loses theirs.
7467-the-newcomes-memoirs-of-a-most-resp:
William Makepeace Thackeray, edited here by his own fictional stand-in Arthur Pendennis, tells the story of the Newcomes, a most respectable family. Colonel Newcome, back from India with wild oats behind him, anchors the tale, while his son Clive grows up, goes to school, and tries to become a painter. Around them gather uncles, aunts, and cousins, all fiercely concerned with respectability.

Ethel Newcome, the colonel's granddaughter, stands at the novel's heart, torn between love and the family's ambitions for her. Chapters carry the reader from London drawing rooms to Rome and back to Pall Mall, among painters, lords, and schemers. The Newcomes is Thackeray's great family saga after Vanity Fair: funny, sad, and unsparing about what respectability costs.
75041-his-to-fly:
An aviation story by Richard Howells Watkins. Its headnote states the problem in three lines. One parachute and two men, and the ship cannot land. The scene is a New Jersey meadow after the Great War. A five-year-old biplane waits at the field's edge. Jerry Tabor, thin and sandy-haired, rigs her wires with pliers.

His partner Beak Becket arrives in full pilot regalia. Leather coat, knickers, and shining puttees impress nobody at a barnstorming field. Beak scolds Jerry for test-hopping the machine. A mere wing walker, he sneers, knows nothing of flying. Jerry answers that he is a pilot too, or their act took money under false pretences. Watkins writes the barnstormers' rivalry from inside the trade.
76617-too-old-to-fly:
Ivan March wrote this war story about Sergeant Horatio Galladay, a marine machine gunner said in the headnote to be too old to fly. Galladay learned his trade from the rear end of a mule. Outnumbered, his pilot shot and himself wounded, the old sergeant keeps up his stream of lead as the plane falls.

The story first gives Galladay's schooling: a grammar-school course in the Spanish-American War at the crank of a Gatling gun. High school came in the Philippines, and a navy cross for his studies. A Moro chieftain once carved his initials on Galladay's body when the gun jammed and the Colt ran empty, and Galladay dropped him with a straight right to the jaw. Service in Haiti, San Domingo, Nicaragua, China, and Vera Cruz followed, with bullet wounds and a flattened nose, before the World War found the sergeant ready for the air.
76888-before-the-most-holy:
Mother Mary Loyola of the Bar Convent, York, wrote Before the Most Holy, in Latin Coram Sanctissimo, edited by Father Thurston. Herder published it at St Louis in 1904, with Cardinal Vaughan's imprimatur of September 1900. The book is dedicated to Jesus Christ, yesterday, today, and the same for ever. The preface calls the custom of paying visits to the Blessed Sacrament a striking example of development. It means development in Catholic devotional practice.

Down to the later Middle Ages, the preface notes, such usage seems to have been entirely unknown. Mother Loyola wrote many loved books of devotion. This one teaches the visit: prayer before the tabernacle, in short meditations.
77124-here-foloweth-a-lytell-treatyse-of:
A little Tudor treatise on the beauty of women, first published around 1525, survives here in its old spelling. The translator says he turned it from French into English at a gentleman's desire, and he asks Mary, daughter of Saint Anne, to guide his hand. He confesses, in verse, that he has little practice in judging women's beauty, being an unpleasant page kept from great company.

Still, he writes, no man with more practice will take the pains, and the thing deserves memory. Beauty, he argues, caused Troilus to love Cressida, Paris to love Helen, Achilles to love Polyxena, and Tristan to love Isolde. The rules follow in verse: beauty asks first for a simple manner and countenance, since a haughty bearing turns beauty to displeasure. The book is a curious relic of courtly taste, part compliment and part conduct rule.
7767-the-graymouse-family:
Nellie M. Leonard's The Graymouse Family follows a mouse household through ten short chapters for young readers. Mother Graymouse keeps school, Uncle Squeaky tells stories, Limpy-Toes gets lost, Buster faces chocolates, and Silver Ears sets out on an adventure of her own.

Visits to Mrs. Field-Mouse, moving days, and a Christmas tree round out the family year, while Thomas Cat prowls near at hand. Pictures show Ruth and Robert, Grand-daddy Whiskers with warm biscuits, and a busy march to the barn. It is a gentle animal tale of home, kin, and small perils.
77690-a-bold-bad-butterfly:
A Bold Bad Butterfly and Other Fables and Verses is a book of light verse by Oliver Herford, published in London by Gay and Bird in 1906. Herford drew the many pictures himself. The title piece opens the contents, followed by Crumbs and The Silver Question.

The fables that follow keep the menagerie whimsical. How the Lion Became King, The Wakeful Princess, and A Corner in Curls lead the list. A Butterfly of Fashion and The Boastful Butterfly return to the title insect. The Snail's Dream, The Tragic Mice, and The Untutored Giraffe fill the middle pages. Herford was the wittiest illustrator poet of his day on both sides of the Atlantic. His nonsense fables moralize gently, in couplets and drawings made to be laughed over first.
78136-the-boy-who-couldn-t-fly:
Charles Verral wrote The Boy Who Couldn't Fly, a tale of a lame boy and an airplane. Dan Sutherland watches a red monoplane skim over his town of Newton and burns to be in it.

The plane is a Ross Comet, and Dan names its wing shape and landing gear at a glance. His friend Murph sees only another crate. Dan's father, president of the bank, hates flying and calls it unthinkable. His eyes drop to Dan's right leg, crippled and held in a steel brace. That glance says all: pity. Dan wants the sky because no one pities a pilot. Verral builds a boy's fight for freedom on that longing.
78222-the-crimson-butterfly:
Edmund Snell wrote The Crimson Butterfly, first published in London in 1924. The coming of Abu-Samar opens the tale, and a dance at Rembakut sets its Borneo stage. James Armourer, the hero, entertains early and asserts himself as the strange events gather.

A professor turns naturalist over a strange insect, and tragedy strikes at Bukit-Serang. Joyce displays curiosity, colleagues confer, and a nocturnal expedition follows, then a second victim. Mrs Battiscombe disappears, a hut in the trees is found, and a goddess of the butterfly is named. The antidote, the breeding-house trap, and the temple of the crimson butterfly bring the hunt to its end. Snell mixes jungle mystery with the detective form, in the rich manner of his many Eastern tales.
79662-the-gist-of-burton-s-anatomy-of-me:
Finger wrote the Gist of Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, in 1924. It stands number 763 in a series of little blue books. Haldeman-Julius edited that series from Girard in Kansas. Burton's great book is more talked about than read, it opens. Browne's meditations share that case, it adds.

Milton and Fuller share that neglect too. Yet the Anatomy is readable, the gist insists throughout. Printed in 1642, it shows no hint of the archaic, it says. Inventive wit and scattered learning tag it correctly, he holds. A quaintness and a special charm delight in its pages. Doctor Johnson owed much to that old thunderer, it owns. Could a great tower fall into neglect and be forgotten, it asks. Highways of print suffer the same fate as buildings here. Finger gives the everyday reader Burton in an hour.
9330-the-biography-of-a-grizzly:
Ernest Seton-Thompson wrote this biography of a grizzly in 1899, with seventy-five drawings. The book tells the history of Wahb, a bear of the Palette Ranch on the Graybull, gathered from hunter, miner, personal experience, and the ranch host himself. Grace Gallatin Seton-Thompson designed title, cover, and makeup.

Drawings show cubs rushing like little pigs, a bear treed till morning, and a savage bobcat warned off. Seton's tale follows Wahb from cub to king of the range. The book remains a classic of animal biography, true to wild life and full of frontier color.
a-visit-to-the-holy-land-egypt-and-italy: Ida Pfeiffer visits the Holy Land, Egypt, and Italy in this travel volume, translated from the German by H. W. Dulcken. The journey departs from Vienna by steamer down the Danube, past Pesth, Belgrade, and the Iron Gate, to Constantinople and Beyrout. The journey takes in residence at Jerusalem, Bethlehem, a ride through the wilderness to the Dead Sea, Nazareth, and the bazaar at Damascus. They carry a determined traveller through lands most readers knew only from books.
britannica-1911-acromegaly:
Acromegaly is a disease of overgrowth. Its name joins Greek words for point and large. Bone and soft parts both enlarge truly. The terminal parts of the body suffer most. Face, hands, and feet grow out of proportion. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the basic clinical picture. Women between twenty-five and forty are most often affected. Men suffer the disease less frequently.

Cause was linked to one small gland. Disturbance of the pituitary gland is generally blamed. Doctors tried pituitary extract as a treatment. That trial belonged to the new organo-therapy. Thyroid extract was also tried, on analogy with myxoedema. It brought no marked success, the entry admits. Readers get an honest snapshot of early endocrinology.
britannica-1911-alder-fly:
Alder-fly names insects of the family Sialidae, as explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They are neuropterous insects, a group of net-winged kinds, related to the ant-lions. Long, thread-like antennae and four large wings mark the adults, the front pair rather longer than the hind pair. Their life, though, is mostly spent in the water.

Females lay a vast number of eggs on grass stems near water. The larvae that hatch are aquatic, active hunters armed with strong, sharp jaws. They breathe through seven pairs of feathery gill filaments along the abdomen, a feature the entry stresses. When full-grown they leave the water and pass a quiet pupal stage on land before emerging as winged adults. Sialis lutaria is the well-known British example. American genera Corydalis and Chauliodes are remarkable for their giant size and sabre-like jaws.
britannica-1911-anomaly:
Anomaly, in the 1911 Britannica, is a term entry that moves from plain speech to the stars. In plain use it means a break from the common rule, from a Greek word for unevenness. In astronomy it names the angle of a body from the near point of its orbit. The entry sets out three kinds with care. True anomaly is the real angle at the focus of the orbit.

Mean anomaly is the angle the body would have at a steady rate of motion. Eccentric anomaly is read off a circle drawn round the orbit. Kepler's problem, finding a planet's place from its mean anomaly, was solved in part by Kepler and more fully by later men. The entry adds the anomalistic year, from one perihelion to the next, 25 minutes longer than a tropical year.
britannica-1911-bareilly:
Bareilly is a city and district of British India, in the Rohilkhand division of the United Provinces. The city stands on the Ramganga river, 812 miles north-west of Calcutta by rail, and held 131,208 people in 1901. Two mosques of the 1600s, a modern fort over the cantonments, and the palace of the nawab of Rampur are among its buildings named.

The city is an army headquarters and a rail junction, and its chief manufactures are furniture and upholstery. Bareilly college teaches to Calcutta University degree level with an English staff. The district covers 1,580 square miles of level, fertile, well-watered country. The 1911 Britannica entry adds the tarai, a forest belt along its north teeming with tigers, bears, deer, and wild pigs.
britannica-1911-beauly:
Beauly, a town in Inverness shire, Scotland, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The name is a worn form of a French word for fair place. The town stands on the river Beauly, ten miles west of Inverness by rail. Its population in 1901 was 855, the entry gives.

Its chief interest is the fair remains of a priory founded in 1230 for Cistercian monks. At the Reformation the buildings passed to Lord Lovat, save the church, now a ruin. Across the river is the site of Lovat Castle, once held by another family. Three miles south stands Beaufort Castle, the chief seat of the Lovats. It is a fine modern house in the Scots baronial style, on the site of an older fortress.
britannica-1911-beaumont-family:
Beaumont is a family history article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name, also given as Belmont or Bellomont, came from Beaumont le Roger in Normandy. Early in the eleventh century Roger de Beaumont married a daughter of the count of Meulan. Their son Robert became count of Meulan in about 1080.

The entry says Robert had fought at Hastings before that date. He gained wide estates in Warwickshire on top of his Norman lands. Under William the Second and Henry the First he rose to high standing. Henry in particular owed much to him for the English crown, the article states. Robert gained lands in Leicestershire and held some rights of an earl. Still, the claim that he was made earl of Leicester is called an error.
britannica-1911-berkeley-family:
Berkeley is the name of an ancient English family, famed for holding its feudal castle by the Severn on the lands that gave it the name. Sure descent runs from Robert fitz Harding, who died in 1170. Old pedigree-makers made his father Harding a young son of a Danish king; modern historians instead find an English thane of Somerset in Domesday Book.

Robert, a rich Bristol man, backed Henry of Anjou and won the Berkeley manor by charter in 1153. The long entry then follows the lords through wars, marriages and peerage tangles. Castles were seized under King John. A childless lord hacked the great estates apart. The fifth earl’s honours make the last curious chapter. Branches spread widely over the centuries, and the piece is among the longest family histories in the volume.
britannica-1911-bethune-family:
