The Bethune family were lords of Bethune and sworn guards of the great abbey of Saint-Vaast at Arras from the 1000s. From them sprang a great French house. Its branches gave France the dukes of Sully, Charost, Orval, and Ancenis. It also gave marquises, counts, and princes of note. Conon de Bethune, the crusader and poet, was an early forebear of the line.

The most famed member of the house was Maximilien, baron of Rosny and later duke of Sully. He served as minister to Henry IV. His brother Philip, count of Selles and Charost, was an envoy to Scotland, Rome, Savoy, and Germany. He died in 1649. Hippolyte de Bethune left the king a rich store of papers on the past and works of art at his death in 1665. The Charost branch gave France a run of generals in the 1600s and 1700s.
britannica-1911-caerphilly:
Caerphilly is a market town in Glamorganshire in Wales, set out in a 1911 Britannica town entry. It lies seven miles from Cardiff and twelve from Newport by rail and road. The source of its name is not known, the entry states at the start. Its urban district held more than fifteen thousand people in 1901.

Rail links grew in steps, with a tunnel giving a direct line to Cardiff in 1871. A branch to Senghenydd opened in 1894 to serve coal country nearby. The town grew from old parishes joined into one district in 1893. Readers get dates, lines, and counts that show a coal age town taking shape.
britannica-1911-capercally:
Capercally is a bird, the largest of the grouse family, and this 1911 Britannica entry deals first with its name and its old range. The name is commonly tied to Gaelic words for a horse and a wood, though one scholar prefers a root meaning an old man, and so an old bird. The bird's Latin name is Tetrao urogallus, and it was once native to Scotland and Ireland. English names for it include wood-grouse and cock-of-the-wood.

The spelling of the name varies a great deal across writers. The first notice of the bird as a dweller in North Britain comes in the works of Hector Boethius, printed in 1526. Scottish writers mention it over the next two hundred years, yet plainly knew it little. Only Bishop Lesley, in 1578, gave it a definite home, in Ross, Lochaber, and other mountain districts.
britannica-1911-carloman-king-of-bavaria:
Carloman (828–880) was king of Bavaria and Italy. He was the eldest son of Louis the German. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. In 856 he took charge of Bavaria's eastern frontier. He campaigned against the Bohemians and Moravians with fame. He married a daughter of Count Ernest of the Bohemian mark. In 861 he joined his father-in-law in resisting his own father.

For years Carloman swung between rebellion and submission. In 865 a settlement gave him Bavaria and Carinthia as his share. He stayed loyal while his younger brothers troubled their father. His Moravian war ended in Frankish supremacy by 874. In 875 the emperor Louis II named him heir in Italy. Charles the Bald cajoled him out of that claim for the time. In 876 he became king of Bavaria in fact. In 877 he was crowned king of the Lombards at Pavia.
britannica-1911-carrara-family:
Carrara is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a powerful family of Longobard origin, also called the Carraresi, who ruled Padua in the fourteenth century. They took their name from the village of Carrara near Padua, and their first recorded member, Gamberto, died before 970. In the wars of Guelphs and Ghibellines they began on the Ghibelline side and later crossed to the Guelphs.

That switch brought war with Ezzelino da Romano, and one Jacopo da Carrara drowned fleeing his siege. A later Jacopo fought Cangrande della Scala of Verona, was taken prisoner, yet negotiated peace in 1318, and the Paduans then elected him their lord to end civil strife. His nephew Marsiglio, famed for cunning, handed Padua to Cangrande and later seized it back with Venetian troops in 1337. The entry follows these bargains and betrayals through the family's hold on the city.
britannica-1911-cicely:
Cicely, Myrrhis odorata, in the natural order Umbelliferae, is a perennial herb with a leafy hollow stem two to three feet high. Its leaves are much divided and whitish beneath, with a large sheathing base at the stem. Small white flowers stand in terminal umbels, heads borne at the ends of the stems. Only the outer flowers of those heads are fertile, the entry notes as a mark of the plant.

Fruit is dark brown, long and narrow, and beaked in shape, at three quarters of an inch to one inch. The plant is a native of central and southern Europe, growing wild in the entry's account. In parts of England and Scotland it is found in pastures, usually near houses. Aromatic and stimulant properties belong to it, and it was formerly used as a pot-herb in cooking.
britannica-1911-cinna-family:
Cinna was a Roman patrician family of the Cornelian house, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its most marked member was Lucius Cornelius Cinna, a backer of Marius in his fight with Sulla. After service in the war with the Marsi he was made consul in the year 87 before Christ. He had sworn to Sulla that he would make no revolt.

He broke that oath, joined Marius, raised an army of Italians, and took the city of Rome. His entry was marked by a slaughter of the friends of Sulla. Marius died soon after, and Cinna ruled on with new colleagues. In the year 84 he was still consul and was forced to march out against Sulla. As he shipped his troops to meet Sulla in Thessaly, his own men rose and killed him. His daughter Cornelia was the wife of Julius Caesar.
britannica-1911-clare-family:
Clare is the name of a famous English family that played a great part in England, Wales and Ireland, in Freeman's words. Its ancestor was Count Godfrey, eldest illegitimate son of Richard the Fearless, duke of Normandy. Godfrey's son Gilbert of Brionne had two sons, Richard and Baldwin, who both accompanied the Conqueror to England. Richard, called of Bienfaite, of Tunbridge or of Clare, founded the house of Clare.

Richard took his English name from his strongholds at Tunbridge and at Clare, whose castle mounds still remain on the Essex and Suffolk borders. Clare headed his great honour, lying chiefly in the eastern counties. As joint justiciar in the king's absence he helped suppress the revolt of 1075. Through his wife Rohese, Giffard estates later came to his house. His five sons founded lines including the FitzWalters.
britannica-1911-clovelly:
Clovelly is a fishing village in Devonshire, England, eleven miles west-south-west of Bideford, holding 621 people in 1901. Old-fashioned cottages cluster in a unique position on the sides of a rocky cleft in the north coast. Its main street resembles a staircase descending 400 feet to the pier, too steeply for any wheeled traffic. Thick woods shelter the village on three sides from the coastal weather.

That shelter renders the climate so mild that fuchsias and other delicate plants flourish in midwinter. All Saints' church, restored in 1866, is late Norman and holds monuments to the Carys, lords of the manor for 600 years. Surrounding scenery is famous for its richness of colour, especially in the grounds of Cary Court and along the Hobby road. Dickens described Clovelly in A Message from the Sea, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-colonna-family:
The Colonna are a noble Roman family, second only to the Gaetani in age and first among Roman houses in weight. Four early popes are said to have come from its line. Its firm pedigree starts with Pietro, lord of Colonna, Palestrina and Paliano, about the year 1100. He was likely a brother of Pope Benedict IX. Three branch lines grew from his stock.

In the 1100s the family held the counts of Tusculum rank. Its feuds with the Orsini and Gaetani mark the Rome of that age. Like other great lords of the Campagna, the Colonna robbed travellers and towns. They did not spare the pope when they felt wronged. Boniface VIII struck back with excommunication to break their power. The entry closes with the family palace in Rome. Martin V began it, and it holds a rich store of pictures and sculpture.
britannica-1911-dance-family:
Dance is the name of an English family marked in architecture, art, and the drama. George Dance the elder (1700–1768), architect to the city of London, designed the Mansion House in 1739 and churches at Aldgate, Old Street, and Shoreditch. His eldest son James took the name Love and acted at Drury Lane for twelve years. James also wrote plays. A third son, Nathaniel, painted portraits and history pieces.

Nathaniel Dance-Holland studied in Italy, helped found the Royal Academy, and painted George III and his queen for its first show. Rich by marriage, he left art for parliament and a baronetcy. The youngest son, George Dance the younger, followed his father as city architect in 1768. He had already shown designs for Blackfriars Bridge in 1761. The entry closes with Charles Dance, a writer of farces for Madame Vestris.
britannica-1911-ely:
Ely is a cathedral city and market-town in Cambridgeshire, England, 16 miles north-north-east of Cambridge, with 7713 people in 1901. It stands on a rise on the west bank of the Ouse, in the Isle of Ely, above the flat fens. The great cathedral towers over the town as a landmark for miles.

The entry gives the town's trade in market gardening, tobacco pipes, and earthenware, and notes St Mary's church and the grammar school founded by Henry VIII in 1541. Ely's fame rests on Etheldreda, who founded a religious house here in 673 and became its first abbess. The Danes destroyed that house in 870, and a Benedictine monastery rose in its place in 970. The present cathedral was begun by its first Norman abbot, Simeon, in 1083. For centuries the abbot, and later the bishop, held near-total power in the town.
britannica-1911-faithfull-emily:
English philanthropist Emily Faithfull, born at Headley Rectory in Surrey in eighteen thirty five, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the youngest daughter of a clergyman. She took a great interest in the conditions of working women. Their sphere of labour was then painfully limited, the entry notes.

In eighteen sixty she set up a printing house for women in London, to widen that sphere. The Victoria Press soon won a name for its excellent work. She was then appointed printer and publisher to Queen Victoria. In eighteen sixty three she began a monthly magazine. For eighteen years it urged the claims of women to paid work without pause. She also lectured widely in England and the United States, and published a novel.
britannica-1911-family:
Family is the subject of a long study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The piece starts with the word itself and its roots in Roman law. The Latin word familia first meant the slaves of a master. It then grew to cover all his goods, and at last all kin who traced descent from one stock.

The study then sets out a plain sense of the modern family. It is the small group formed by one man, one woman, and their children. Old records from Israel, India, Greece, and Rome are called as proof. Each shows the family in place at the dawn of written history. The piece treats it as the seed from which wider society grew.
britannica-1911-frederick-iii-king-of-si:
Frederick III (1272-1337), king of Sicily, was the third son of Peter of Aragon and of Constance, daughter of Manfred. When his brother James took Aragon in 1291, Frederick stayed as regent of Sicily. James then bargained the island away in 1295, handing it back to the Church and the Angevins, but the Sicilians refused to be returned to the French they had expelled in 1282.

Crowned at Palermo in 1296, Frederick reformed the government and widened the powers of the Sicilian parliament. War followed: his fleet was beaten off Cape Orlando, yet he captured Philip of Anjou in 1299, and plague broke the invasion of Charles of Valois. The treaty of Caltabellotta in 1302 recognised him as king of Trinacria for his lifetime. Later wars, a papal interdict from 1321 to 1335, and fresh Angevin raids filled his reign. He died in 1337, and his son Peter followed him in spite of the treaty.
britannica-1911-gregory-family:
Gregory is the name of a Scottish family famed in science, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives notices of its leading members. Many of the family won high eminence in varied fields, fourteen of them holding professorships in mathematics or medicine. The entry begins with David Gregory (1627-1720).

David, it says, gave his poorer neighbors the free benefit of his medical skill, and was the first man in the north of Scotland to own a barometer. His weather forecasts by it drew a witchcraft charge, which he talked his way out of. His younger brother James (1638-1675) follows, the mathematician who published in 1663 the treatise that made known his reflecting telescope.
britannica-1911-hastings-family:
Hastings, a famous English family, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. John, Baron Hastings, who lived from about 1262 to about 1313, opens the account. He was a son of Sir Henry de Hastings, called to Parliament as a baron by Simon de Montfort in 1264. Sir Henry led the Londoners at Lewes and was taken prisoner at Evesham.

After his release Sir Henry kept up his fight against Henry the Third and made a last stand in the Isle of Ely. He submitted in July 1267. His son John wed Isabella, daughter of the earl of Pembroke, and fought in Scotland and Wales. Through his mother he inherited the lordship of Abergavenny. In 1290 Hastings came forward as a claimant for the Scottish throne. He failed, yet stayed loyal to Edward the First.
britannica-1911-howard-family:
The Howards have long held the first place among English families. Their head, the duke of Norfolk, is first of the dukes and hereditary earl marshal of England. The earls of Suffolk, Carlisle and Effingham carry the younger lines in the peerage. The founder was a Norfolk lawyer, William Howard, summoned to parliament as a justice in 1295 and made a justice of the common pleas in 1297.

Over that founder's parentage genealogists have argued for centuries. Pedigree-makers have claimed him in turn for a Norman earl's line and for Hereward, the last of the English. The Norfolk deeds gathered for Thomas, earl of Arundel, in the early 17th century point plainer: he sprang from a Norfolk family holding lands at Wiggenhall. The long article traces the house from those small roots through the dukes of Norfolk, their attainders and restorations, to its full modern spread.
britannica-1911-humbert-ranieri-carlo-em:
Humbert the First, king of Italy, who lived from 1844 to 1900, was the son of Victor Emmanuel the Second. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Turin on the fourteenth of March 1844. Fine teachers trained him, among them Massimo d'Azeglio. He entered the army in 1858 with the rank of captain. He stood in the battle of Solferino in 1859. In 1866 he led a division at Custozza.

Near Villafranca, Austrian horse charged his men, and Humbert formed them into squares. He stayed in the square most open to attack and beat the charge off. A gold medal for valour marked that day. In 1868 he wed his cousin Margherita of Savoy. Their son, born in 1869, became Victor Emmanuel the Third. Humbert took the throne at his father's death in January 1878.
britannica-1911-july: July is the seventh month in the Christian calendar and has thirty one days. It was at first the fifth month, and the Romans called it Quintilis. The later name Julius honours Julius Caesar, who was born in the month. The Anglo Saxons called it hay month or mead month, since the meadows were then in bloom. Chief dates kept in it are the Dog Days from the 3rd, St Swithin on the 15th, and St James on the 25th.
britannica-1911-keith-family:
Keith is the name of an old Scottish family that took its name from the barony of Keith in East Lothian. The lands were said to have been granted by Malcolm II to a member of the house for service against the Danes. The office of great marishal of Scotland, later hereditary in the family, may have been granted at the same time.

The office and the lands were confirmed to Sir Robert Keith by a charter of King Robert Bruce. Sir Robert led the Scottish horse at Bannockburn and was killed at Neville's Cross in 1346. At the close of the 14th century Sir William Keith gained the crag of Dunnottar in Kincardineshire by an exchange of lands. He built Dunnottar Castle there, and it became the stronghold of his line. A later Sir William was made Lord Keith in 1430.
britannica-1911-kidwelly:
Kidwelly is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a small Welsh borough in Carmarthenshire. It stands where two streams, the Gwendraeth Fawr and the Gwendraeth Fach, meet near Carmarthen Bay. The count of 1901 gave it 2,285 people. The article calls it a decayed market town.

Its chief glory is its castle, one of the finest in South Wales. The castle dates mostly from the thirteenth century and stands on a knoll above the stream. The parish church of Saint Mary is of the fourteenth century, with a tall tower and spire. Yet the quiet town has a stirred past. William de Londres first raised a castle here, and in 1135 Gwenllian, wife of a Welsh prince, attacked the place in force.
britannica-1911-kisfaludy-karoly:
Károly Kisfaludy (1788–1830) was a Hungarian author, born at Téte, near Raab, on the 6th of February 1788. His birth cost his mother her life and won him his father's lasting hatred. He joined the army as a cadet in 1804, served in Italy, Servia and Bavaria, and rose to first lieutenant. In 1812 he left the army, studied painting at Vienna, and lived for years in poverty, writing as he went.

His drama Ilka, staged at Fehérvár and Buda in 1819, made him famous and set him on his true path. The Voivode Stiber and The Petitioners followed, among the first dramas written in Magyar. Under the critic Kazinczy he learned to refine his style, and through his friend Gaal he came to Shakespeare and Goethe. He stands here as the creator of the Hungarian drama.
britannica-1911-lacewing-fly: Lacewing-fly is the name for neuropterous insects of the families Hemerobiidae and Chrysopidae, kin to the ant-lions and scorpion-flies. They have long thread-like antennae, longish bodies and two pairs of large, similar, richly veined wings. The larvae are short grubs set with hair-tufts and tubercles. They feed on aphids, or green fly, and cover themselves with the emptied skins of their prey. Lacewings of the genus Chrysopa are commonly called golden-eye flies.
britannica-1911-lantern-fly: Lantern-fly names large insects of the genus Fulgora and its kin. Bright colours mark the group. A hollow growth like a snout fronts the head. That growth can match the rest of the body in size. It was long said to shine at night. Marie Sibylle de Merian backed the claim. Linnaeus spread it through light-based names. Later watching found no glow. The claim is now held in doubt.
britannica-1911-lindsay-family:
Lindsay is the family name of the earls of Crawford, and a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the house. The family is of great age in Scotland. Its first known man there was Sir Walter de Lindesia. He came north early in the twelfth century with David, later king of Scots.

The entry tells how the stock split into three branches. Their lands lay in both Scotland and England. The heads of all three sat as barons in the Scottish parliament for over two hundred years. In 1398 the chief of the house was raised to an earldom. The Lindsays long held the hill district of Crawford, from which the title takes its name.
britannica-1911-locri-italy:
Locri was a Greek city of Magna Graecia in Italy. First settlers held the Zephyrian cape, Capo Bruzzano. Three or four years on, they moved twelve miles north, near modern Gerace. The name Locri Epizephyrii stuck all the same. Founding is set about 683 B.C.

First of Greek towns, Locri gained a written law code. Zaleucus gave it in 664 B.C. Offshoot towns Meisma and Hipponium sprang from it. Croton's attack broke on the river Sagras. Syracuse stood by it against Rhegium. Pindar sang its upright ways in two Olympic odes. Dionysius I wed a Locrian wife, and the town grew fat and wide-walled. Freedom went with that growth. From Heraclea's fight to 205 B.C. it flipped sides between Rome and her foes. Scipio took it in that year.
britannica-1911-marcellus-family:
Marcellus was the name of a Roman plebeian house in the Claudian clan. The 1911 Britannica article gives short lives of its best known men. First comes Marcus Claudius Marcellus, who lived from about 268 to 208 BC. He was a Roman general in the Second Punic War and the captor of Syracuse. In his first consulship he slew a Gallic chief in single combat. He won the spolia opima, the last time that honour was gained.

After the Roman loss at Cannae, Marcellus held the army remnant together and saved Nola. He then took Syracuse after a siege of two years, in spite of the war machines of Archimedes. He spared the people but sent their art to Rome. The article calls him the sword of Rome and notes he was slain in his last consulship.
britannica-1911-philately:
Philately, the study and collecting of postage stamps, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word joins Greek terms for loving and free of tax. The craze for stamps began soon after Britain issued its first penny and two penny stamps in 1840. A British Museum official was among the first to collect them.

By about 1860 collectors had grown systematic in their work. They noted kinds of paper, watermarks, perforation, shades of colour, and the outline of each stamp. A Paris teacher had pupils paste foreign stamps into atlases by country. Dealers appeared, and the first catalogue of stamps came out at Strasburg in 1861. Paris collectors led in measuring stamps and sorting the issues of each land. The first English catalogue soon followed, and clubs for the hobby formed in several countries.
britannica-1911-pole-family:
Pole is the family name of the earls and dukes of Suffolk, and their rise is traced in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. But for the loss of Richard the Third at Bosworth, the house might have given England its next king. Yet its roots lay not in war but in trade. The Poles began as merchants at Kingston upon Hull.

Some have called them the first English peers whose wealth was built on trade. The text notes one older house that may beat that claim. The line starts with William atte Pole, a merchant of Ravensrode who settled in Hull. His sons Richard and William grew famed for wealth at a time when the Crown had great need of rich men help. Richard moved to London and served as the king butler. The entry shows trade cash turned into rank and power.
britannica-1911-roger-i-of-sicily:
Roger the First of Sicily is a royal life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Norman ruler of Sicily. He lived from 1031 to 1101 and was the youngest son of Tancred of Hauteville. He reached the south of Italy soon after 1057. The writer Malaterra praised his looks, his height, his cool counsel, and his fury in battle.

Roger shared with his brother Robert Guiscard the conquest of Calabria. By a pact of 1062 the brothers split each castle and town there half and half. Robert then set Roger to the task of taking Sicily. The island held Muslims and also many Greek Christians ruled by Arab princes who had grown near free of the sultan of Tunis. In May 1061 the brothers crossed from Reggio and took Messina.
britannica-1911-roger-ii-of-sicily:
Roger the Second of Sicily, a Norman king, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1093, he began to rule in his own right in 1112. From the first he aimed to join all Norman conquests in Italy. When Duke William of Apulia died with no child in 1127, Roger struck. He claimed all Hauteville lands and the overlordship of Capua too.

Pope Honorius fought that union of Sicily and Apulia lands. At Capua he preached a holy war against the claimant's cause. Robert of Capua and Ranulf, Roger's own kin by marriage, led it. That league failed, and in 1128 the pope gave way in part. At Benevento he set Roger as duke of Apulia by right. Town revolts then bent to his will by the next year.
britannica-1911-rose-family:
Rose is the name of a line of German chemists, traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica across four generations. Valentine Rose the elder (1736–1771) was a Berlin apothecary who found the mix still called Rose's fusible metal. His son Valentine (1762–1807) proved in 1800 that sulphuric ether holds no sulphur.

The younger Valentine left four sons, among them Heinrich and Gustav, both pupils of Berzelius. Heinrich Rose (1795–1864) gave himself to inorganic chemistry and to the craft of analysis. His handbook of analytical chemistry, first out in 1829, ran through six editions and stands as a classic. He also found antimony pentachloride and studied how the mass of water sways reactions. Gustav Rose (born 1798) turned from mining to mineral study, ran the Royal Mineralogical Museum at Berlin, and joined Humboldt's expedition to the Ural and Altai mountains in 1829.
britannica-1911-saw-fly:
Saw fly is the name for a group of insects in the wasp order, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Members have a body part that sits close to the thorax with no narrow waist. That build hides the base of the hind legs. Their feelers vary in shape and in joint count.

Two parts of the egg laying organ are shaped as saws. At rest those saws lie in a sheath made of two other parts. The young are most often caterpillar like, but have more pairs of false legs than moth young. When alarmed they roll into a spiral. The females cut small slits in soft leaf parts with their saws and lay an egg in each. One genus alone forms galls, on willow leaves.
britannica-1911-silly:
Silly, now meaning weakly foolish or stupid, is a word that has much changed its sense, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article traces that change. In Old English the word meant prosperous or happy. It was formed from a root meaning time or season, and so happiness. Kindred words in Icelandic and German mean bliss or blessedness. A Latin word for whole and safe may also be allied.

The meaning slid step by step: happy, blessed, innocent or simple, then helpless, weak, and so foolish. An old Scots word for a caul, the silly-how, keeps the sense of lucky cap. The article compares the path of the word simple, from onefold in Latin to plain, then unlearned and foolish.
britannica-1911-stafford-family:
Stafford is the name of a famed English house of high rank. The 1911 Britannica entry founds the house with Robert, a Norman lord. He came to England at the Conquest with his kin of Tosny. His great fief spread across seven counties of the realm. He took his name from his seat at Stafford Castle there.

The fief owed the king the service of sixty knights in war. When the male line failed, the lands passed by marriage to Hervey Bagot. His heir Edmund was called to Parliament as a baron in 1299. Edmund's son Ralph won fame in the French wars of his age. He held Aiguillon, fought at Crecy, and was made earl in 1351.
britannica-1911-stanley-family:
Stanley is a family history from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an old and famed English house. The family took its name from Stanley in Leek, in the Staffordshire moorlands. Its first known ancestor is Adam de Stanley, of the time of King Stephen. A later William de Stanley won the forestership of Wirral in 1284.

From him came two brothers, Sir William and Sir John Stanley. William's line, the Stanleys of Hooton, held a baronetcy from 1661 until it died out in 1893. John served as lieutenant of Ireland under two kings. He got the Isle of Man from Henry the Fourth and built a fortified house at Liverpool. He wed the heiress of the Lathoms, lords of Lathom and Knowsley. His grandson Thomas fathered the first earl of Derby.
britannica-1911-stone-fly: Stone-fly names medium-sized insects of the family Perlidae, in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They have long, flexible antennae, wide plates under the thorax, and wings like those of grasshoppers in size and shape. The front pair is thin and skin-like rather than leathery, and the hind pair folds like a fan. The young live in water, are active hunters, and look like adults apart from lacking wings and breathing through the skin or tufts laced with air tubes.
britannica-1911-supply: Supply is a word for means set by, and most of all for funds that a law house grants to run the state. In the United Kingdom that grant is the sole right of the House of Commons. Two groups of the House handle it, one for supply and one for ways and means. In Scotland the term once named men charged to rate and take the land tax. Their role grew, then passed to the county groups in eighteen eighty-nine. The entry is a brief note.
britannica-1911-symmachus-family:
Symmachus was the name of a famed Roman family of the fourth to sixth centuries. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it in the gens Aurelia back to 319. One member held the prefecture of Rome in 364 with high honor. The senate gave him a gilded statue for his virtues in 377.

Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, his son, fills most of the account. He rose as champion of the pagan senate against Christian emperors. Banished in 382, he pled in 384 for the altar of Victory return. Ambrose answered him, yet his honesty kept him widely liked. His letters and speeches survive as key remains of that age.
britannica-1911-szombathely:
Szombathely is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Szombathely is the capital of the Hungarian county of Vas. It stands west of Budapest by rail. Its people numbered over twenty three thousand at the census given. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic bishop. Its cathedral, built between 1797 and 1821, has two towers of great height.

The article notes the bishop's palace, with a museum of Roman remains. Other buildings include the county hall, a convent, and a school for priests. The town is a key rail and factory centre, with state rail workshops and mills. It stands on the site of a Roman town that was capital of Pannonia. There a Roman emperor was proclaimed by his legions in the year 193. Many Roman remains have been dug up, from an arena to an aqueduct.
britannica-1911-tancred-sicily:
Tancred is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a king of Sicily who died in 1194. He was a base-born son of Roger, eldest son of King Roger the Second. He was crowned in January 1190 in place of William the Second. The chancellor Matthew and the court clerks backed his claim.

A rival claim came from Constance, daughter of Roger the Second, and her husband Henry. Most nobles backed them, while Tancred had scant support at home. Richard the Lionheart also threatened war at Messina in 1190. Henry had himself crowned emperor at Rome in April 1191. Tancred won the towns over with wide grants of rights. He beat the Apulian barons in the field in 1192 and 1193.
britannica-1911-tinnevelly:
Tinnevelly is a town and district of British India in the Madras presidency. The 1911 Britannica entry sets the town on the Tambraparni river bank. Across the stream lies Palamcottah, the seat of rule for the district. The town held 40,469 souls by the count of 1901. It is the end of a branch line of the South Indian railway.

A temple of Siva with fine carved work forms its chief sight. The district spans 5,389 square miles of land in all. Most of it is a plain some 200 feet above the sea. That plain slopes east with slight rolls in its flat surface. Short streams water it, the Tambraparni first at 80 miles long.
britannica-1911-water-lily:
Water-lily is a name loosely given to near any floating plant with showy flowers. More strictly it means kinds of two genera and their kin in one plant order. The 1911 Britannica entry sets out the build of these water plants in plain terms.

Thick fleshy roots or tubers sit in the mud. Round shield shaped leaves rise to the top of the water, with bare stalks that each bear a single flower. Those flowers show four or five outer leaves and a crowd of inner leaves that grade into a throng of male parts with no sharp line. The seed case holds many parts fused as one, with a flat top of many rays, like a poppy head.
britannica-1911-westerly:
Westerly is a township in Washington County in Rhode Island, at the far south west of the state. The Pawcatuck river parts it from Connecticut and forms its north edge too. Its count of folk in nineteen ten was just past eight thousand. Small towns lie within it, linked by electric cars.

Watch Hill is noted for sea baths, and a fort guards the sound near by. The heart of work is stone. Three kinds of granite are cut near the towns and used for tombs and big builds. Cloth, thread, and print presses are also made. The first homes date to sixteen sixty-one.
britannica-1911-zahringen-family:
Zahringen is the name of an old and strong German family. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the house to its end in 1218. The name comes from a castle and village near Freiburg. The first known member was a count in the Breisgau.

His son Bertold gained a duke title in Carinthia in 1061. That honor proved empty, and revolt soon cost him it. A later Bertold took the duke of Zahringen title in full. The house gained Burgundy land and a rector post there. Its dukes often rode with the emperor in Italy. The last duke founded the town of Bern in Switzerland. When he died in 1218 the main line died out. Split lands passed in part to Habsburg hands. The Baden ruling house still descends from this stock.
by-the-ionian-sea-notes-of-a-ramble-in-s:
By the Ionian Sea records George Gissing's solitary ramble through southern Italy. Gissing leaves Naples under a grey sirocco sky and sails for Paola, on the Calabrian coast. His hosts think the wild south a strange place for an Englishman to wander alone. He goes for the mountains, the sea, and the classical past.

Chapters visit Taranto, Cotrone, Catanzaro, Squillace, and Reggio, among other towns. He seeks the grave of Alaric, the Goth king buried in a river bed. He recalls Cassiodorus, the Roman statesman who retired to these shores. Along the way he notes poverty, fever, dialect, and the kindness of doctors and peasants. The result is a meditative travel book, half guide and half elegy for ancient Magna Graecia.
catalogue-of-the-william-loring-andrews-:
Addison Van Name catalogued the early books that William Loring Andrews gave to Yale University, in an edition of 300 copies printed in 1913. Two manuscripts open the list, a life of Carlo Zeno and a Livy, before the printed books begin with a Latin Bible from Mainz dated 1462.

Entries then run through the great early presses of Germany, Italy, France, and England: Justinian, Isidore, Pliny, Aesop, Ovid, Plato's letters, and Caxton's Polychronicon among them. Each entry gives place, printer, and date, then a full account of leaves, type, columns, and woodcuts. The catalogue doubles as a short history of printing's first sixty years told through one collector's shelves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
The Archconfraternity of the Holy Family began with Henri Belletable, an Engineers' Corps officer at Liège in Belgium. Contact with workmen moved him to labour for their betterment, which he saw could come only through religion. He resolved to found a society divided into companies of twelve in military fashion, and its first meeting took place on Whit Monday evening in 1844 in a carpenter's room.

When numbers outgrew the room, the Redemptorists lent an oratory, and Father Victor Dechamps, Belletable's director, took on this work and became its soul. He carried it to Bishop von Bommel, who approved it formally on 13 February 1845. The bishop erected it as the Confraternity of the Holy Family on 7 April, and stayed its lifelong promoter. Pius IX approved its statutes in 1847, raised it to an archconfraternity, enriched it with indulgences, and placed its rector under the Redemptorists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arundell-fami:
The Arundell family, a very old Norman family long settled in Cornwall from about the mid-thirteenth century, is traced here through Thomas, first Lord Arundell of Wardour. He was born in 1560 and dead at Oxford on 7 November 1639. Son of Sir Matthew Arundell at Wardour Castle, Wiltshire, Thomas was grandson of Sir John Arundell of Lanherne, of the Great Arundells, a Catholic branch. Sir John became Catholic through Father Cornelius of Bodmin, and for defending Cornelius was imprisoned nine years in Ely Palace, Holborn.

Thomas, called the Valiant, strongly opposed reformers and refused Protestant services, for which Elizabeth imprisoned him in 1580. Freed, he travelled and entered Austrian service under Archduke Matthias, Emperor Rudolph II's brother, distinguishing himself in war. The entry follows a recusant family, Catholics who refused the established church, through prison, exile, and soldiering in a confessional age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-o-rei:
Bernard O'Reilly, an Irish-American historian and chaplain, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in County Mayo in 1820, he died in New York in 1907 after emigrating young to Canada and entering Laval University in 1836. Ordained at Quebec in 1843, he served parishes along the St. Lawrence.

He was among the priests who tended Irish emigrants dying of typhus in sheds after the famine year of 1847. Later a Jesuit at Fordham, he served as chaplain with the Irish Brigade in the American Civil War. His histories of the Church and of Ireland made him a popular Catholic writer of his generation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bologna-italy:
Bologna, chief city of its Italian province, grew from the Etruscan Felsina into the Roman colony Bononia. Augustus enlarged and beautified it, and after the Goths fell it joined Ravenna's exarchate in 536. Pepin's donation made it papal territory, though ninth-century turmoil tore it from the popes, and Otto I restored its self-government.

The city backed the popes against the emperors, won recognition of its freedom from Henry V in 1122, and joined the Lombard League. Guelph and Ghibelline factions then split it, and its men captured King Enzo at Fossalto in 1249, holding him prisoner until his death. Later sections cover Christianity in Bologna and its churches, after centuries under the Pepoli, Visconti, and Bentivoglio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capua-italy:
Capua is a city of southern Italy in the province of Caserta, founded by Etruscans and once known as Volturnum. In its early days it served as capital of Campania Felix. Captured by Samnites about 424 B.C., it sought Roman help in 343 B.C. It welcomed Hannibal after Cannae in 216 B.C. Rome retook it in 211 B.C., killing or enslaving its people and declaring its land public.

Julius Caesar later made it a Roman colony called Julia Felix. Vandals sacked it in 456, and Goths, Lombards, and Saracens battered it in turn. Normans under Richard of Aversa took it in 1058, tying its fate to the Two Sicilies. The entry adds Capua's Christian beginnings under St. Priscus. It closes with the archdiocese, its suffragan sees, and a population of 96,800 served by dozens of parishes and hundreds of priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregations:
The entry surveys Holy Family congregations, opening with the Association. Noailles founded it in 1820 to fill the gap Revolutionary ravages left in religious life. Three young ladies began as Sisters of Loreto. It now holds seven congregations, each with distinctive work, garb, and rules, under common constitutions, directed by the Oblates superior general and a directress general. Papal approbation came from 1831, as recently as 1904.

Solitary Sisters lead contemplative lives of adoration and intercession. Taborin founded the Brothers in 1824 in Saint-Claude diocese, gathering five young men for teaching. Memramcook gained Little Sisters in 1874 for temporal care of colleges and seminaries. San Francisco's Sisters date to 1872 under Elizabeth Armer. New Orleans sisters, founded in 1842 by Charles and Delisle, worked among their own race. Siedliska founded the Nazareth sisters in 1874 under Pius IX, running schools for 12,000 pupils, an orphanage, a hospital, and a working-girls' home from Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-of-till:
This biographical entry defends Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, the imperial general of the Thirty Years' War, against centuries of hostile Protestant histories. He was born in Brabant in 1559 and died at Ingolstadt in 1632. Educated by the Jesuits at Cologne, he learned war under Alexander Farnese before surpassing his teacher.

The entry paints him as a man of genuine piety and self-control, a monk in a general's garb. He was honest even to enemies, fatherly to his soldiers, and humane to civilians. Celebrated for caution, grasp of situations, and the training of his troops, he fought from the Rhine to the Seine, in Hungary against the Turks, and as commander of the Catholic League. He died early in the campaign against Gustavus Adolphus. The entry warns against judging him by that unfinished fight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-o-daly:
A biographical entry presents Daniel O'Daly, a diplomatist and historian born in Kerry in 1595 and dead at Lisbon in 1662. From the Desmond Geraldines on his mother's side, he became a Dominican at Tralee. He studied at Burgos, took a doctorate at Bordeaux, and taught theology at Louvain's new Irish Dominican college from 1627.

In 1629 he went to Madrid on college business, won Philip IV's favour, and founded the Irish Dominican college at Lisbon, becoming its first rector. He also built the convent of Bom Successo for Irish Dominican nuns near Lisbon. Kings trusted him as envoy to Charles I, Charles II, Innocent X, and Louis XIV, and his history of Irish Dominicans remains a valued source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donogh-mor-o-:
Donogh Mor O'Daly was a celebrated Irish poet who died in 1244. Some thirty of his poems survive, totaling four or five thousand lines, nearly all on sacred themes. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that O'Reilly and O'Curry style him Abbot of Boyle, though proof that he was a churchman is lacking. His burial in that abbey is certain, and the sacred cast of his verse may account for the title.

O'Donovan names him chief of the Finnyvara O'Dalys in Clare, where his ruined house is still pointed out. For his smooth verse, writers often dub him the Irish Ovid. Second of six brothers, he had a brother Muireadhach the Scotchman who was also a poet, a family of song on both sides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-o-reil:
Edmund O'Reilly was Archbishop of Armagh in a time of war and exile, born at Dublin in 1616 and dead at Saumur in 1669. Trained at Dublin and Louvain, he became vicar-general of Dublin in 1640 and ran that archdiocese from 1642 to 1648 while its archbishop sat on the Confederate council at Kilkenny. The Puritan triumph drove him to prison and then out of Ireland in 1653.

Named to Armagh, he was consecrated at Brussels, yet could not reach his see until 1659, and then only for two years of secret work. He refused the Remonstrance of Peter Walsh, as most Irish bishops did, and Ormond had him jailed and banished. His last years in France were spent caring for Irish colleges abroad, a fitting close to a life lived mostly in exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edouard-branl:
Edouard Branly was a French physicist best known for the coherer, a key part of early wireless telegraphy. Born at Amiens in 1846, he entered the Ecole Normale Superieure in 1865 and taught at Bourges. By 1873 he directed the physics teaching laboratory at the Sorbonne. He took a doctorate on voltaic cells that same year. In 1876 he moved to the Catholic University of Paris.

There he also trained in medicine, taking his degree in 1882, and split his time between healing work and physics. From 1890 he studied thin metal films and loose metal filings near electric sparks. Their resistance changed near a spark. He traced the effect to the waves given off by the spark. His coherer, a tube of filings joining two wires, let a faint signal close a circuit, and it became a core piece of wireless sets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ely:
Ely is an ancient English diocese whose story begins with marshes and eels. Bede writes that Ely lay in East Anglia, a land of about six hundred families, girt by marsh or water and named for its eels. In 649 the district was given to Etheldreda, daughter of King Anna, as dowry on her marriage to Tonbert.

After a second marriage to Egfrid of Northumbria, Etheldreda became a nun. In 673 she founded a monastery at Ely on the site of the present cathedral. She endowed it with her whole island principality. Danes destroyed the house in 870, after it had given the Church four sainted abbesses. Restored for monks alone in 970, it flourished until Abbot Richard proposed a separate see. The pope erected Ely in 1108, and Harvey of Bangor became its first bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family:
Family, in this article, traces its roots to the Latin words famulus and familia. It compares monogamy with polygamy, polyandry, and promiscuity across cultures. Some scholars argued that early humans lived in general promiscuity. Bachofen, Morgan, and McLennan pressed that theory in the nineteenth century.

Westermarck and Letourneau answered that monogamy prevailed from early times. The article cites Genesis and Matthew for the Christian bond of marriage. Limited polygamy appears in some peoples, but monogamy dominates the record. Family life thus rests on a lasting pair bond, not on loose grouping.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foulque-de-ne:
Foulque de Neuilly, who died in March 1202, was a popular preacher of the Crusades and parish priest at Neuilly-sur-Marne near Paris. After what Jacques de Vitry calls a sudden conversion from an irregular life, he went to Paris to study under Pierre, chanter of Notre Dame. His preaching drew large crowds to the Place Champeaux. He denounced usurers and dissolute women in severe terms. The sick were brought to him in hope of cures by laying on of hands and the sign of the cross.

From 1195 he preached around Paris, Normandy, Burgundy, Picardy, and Flanders, and in November 1198 Pope Innocent III charged him with preaching the Fourth Crusade. Foulque later claimed that in three years he had given the cross to 200,000 people. He gave the cross to Boniface of Montferrat at Soissons, entrusted crusade alms to the Cistercians, and died regarded as a saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-peter-:
George Peter Alexander Healy, an American portrait and historical painter born at Boston in 1808, painted more eminent men than any artist of his age. Eldest of five, left fatherless, he began drawing at sixteen, copied a Guido Ecce Homo lent by Miss Stuart, and learned from Sully. At eighteen he began portraits with quick success. In 1834 he sailed for Europe, studying under Gros and Couture for sixteen years and winning a Salon medal in 1840.

His Franklin before Louis XVI took a gold medal at Paris in 1855, the year he settled at Chicago until 1869, then painted twenty-one years in Rome and Paris. Sitters included Pius IX, Lincoln, Grant, Webster, Calhoun, Hawthorne, and Longfellow. His Webster's Reply to Hayne of 1851, now in Faneuil Hall, holds one hundred and thirty portraits. His Reminiscences of a Portrait Painter charms still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homily:
A homily takes its name from the Greek homilia, meaning communion or intercourse with a person, used in that sense in Paul's first letter to Corinth. In Luke and Acts the related verbs mean speaking with someone. In Acts, Paul's long talk at Troas marks the first use of the word for a sermon to Christians joined with the breaking of bread, an informal discourse expounding doctrine.

After that, homily became a mark of Christian worship. Origen first distinguished logos, a formal sermon, from homilia, a tract or commentary. Since Origen, a homily has meant a commentary on some part of Scripture, with no formal introduction, division, or conclusion, aiming to explain its literal sense and draw out its spiritual meaning. It is the oldest form of preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-honore-tourne:
Honoré Tournély was a French theologian, born at Antibes in Provence in 1658 and dead at Paris in 1729. His parents were poor and obscure, but a priest uncle in Paris gave him a good education. He became a doctor of the Sorbonne in 1686. Two years later the king sent him to Douai to teach theology, where his brilliant lectures and zeal against the Jansenists won notice.

Accused of forgeries to compromise the Jansenists, he faced charges never proved. Recalled to Paris, he taught theology at the Sorbonne for twenty-four years, became canon of the Sainte-Chapelle, and received the Abbey of Plainpied. After Clement XI condemned Quesnel's Reflections in the constitution Unigenitus of 1713, Tournély worked hard to win acceptance for it against pamphlets and attacks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-o-reilly:
Hugh O'Reilly was archbishop of Armagh and head of the Confederates of Kilkenny, born in 1580 and dead on Lough Erne's Trinity Island. Turning the national movement into a regular organization was his first conception. At a provincial synod at Kells in March 1642, bishops declared the Irish war for king, religion, and country just and lawful.

Next May he called a national synod at Kilkenny, with prelates and civil lords. After ratifying that declaration, they framed an oath binding adherents to Ireland's fundamental laws, religion's free exercise, and true allegiance to Charles I. They ordered levies of men and money, a mint, an official press, and agents to Catholic courts for aid. They also chartered light vessels under Confederate colours to guard the coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-italy:
Italy wore many ancient names — Saturnia for Saturn, Oenotria as wine land, Ausonia for its Ausonian people, Hesperia as the western land, Tyrrhenia — before Italia itself took hold. The name perhaps comes from a word for calf, marking a land rich in cattle. At first it covered only a small southern strip. That strip was either Calabria's tip or the land between the Sele and Lao later called Lucania. Greek writers of the fifth and fourth centuries before Christ already used it.

By the peace ending the First Punic War in 241 before Christ the name meant peninsular Italy, and by 202, at the Second Punic War's close, it stretched further still. From that naming puzzle the entry grows into a full country survey. It covers land, peoples, history, church, arts, and government. It matches a peninsula whose name outgrew its first small home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-creti:
Journalist and historian Jacques Crétineau-Joly was born at Fontenay-le-Comte on 23 September 1803. He died at Vincennes near Paris on 1 January 1875. He first studied theology at Saint-Sulpice seminary, Paris. Feeling no vocation, he left after three years, having received tonsure. In his twentieth year he became philosophy professor at his hometown college. He soon resigned for ill health.

In 1823 he went to Rome as companion and private secretary to Ambassador Duke of Laval-Montmorency. In 1826 he published Chants romains at Rome, poor verses of irreligious character. After returning home in 1828, he issued poems and dramas, including Les trappistes and Inspirations poétiques. All proved he was no poet. He later turned to journalism and history, where his partisan histories of the Church and Vendée won wider notice. The entry follows a failed poet turned polemic historian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-de-bi:
French scholar Jacques de Billy was a patristic scholar, theologian, jurist, linguist, and Benedictine abbot. He was born at Guise in Picardy in 1535 and died at Paris on 25 December 1581. He began studies at Paris and finished philosophy and theology before eighteen. At his parents' request he then studied law at Orléans and Poitiers. He had no taste for law and gave most time to literature.

His parents' early deaths freed him to pursue letters unhampered. He withdrew to Lyons and later Avignon to study Greek and Hebrew alone. He already held in commendam the abbey of St Léonard of Ferrières and the priory of Taussigny. When his older brother Jean died, further church preferment followed. The entry presents a prodigy of languages who chose monastic scholarship over the bar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Lully, a composer born near Florence in 1633 and dead in Paris in 1687, founded modern French opera from the king's court. Brought to France as a child, his violin gifts won him a place among the king's twenty-four violins and leadership of the private band. He wrote songs, dance music, and court ballets, and reshaped the orchestra.

After study with famed masters, Lully worked with Molière on ballets until 1671, then won control of the Academy of Music in 1672. From 1672 to 1686 he produced twenty operas, among them Isis, Thésée, Armide, and Atys, bettering recitative and inventing the French overture. He also wrote church music, and died from a wound struck while beating time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-boyle-o-:
John Boyle O'Reilly was an Irish poet, novelist, and editor who rose from Fenian prisoner to a leading voice of Catholic America. Born at Drogheda in 1844, he worked as a printer and served as a trooper in the Tenth Hussars. He joined the Fenian movement, was betrayed and court-martialled, and saw a life sentence cut to twenty years' penal servitude in Australia. Study convinced him that constitutional agitation, not force, was the road to Home Rule.

Escaping from Australia in 1869 with the help of a New Bedford whaling captain, he became editor of Boston's Pilot in 1870. He was part proprietor from 1876 until his death in 1890. His books include four volumes of poems, the novel Moondyne drawn from his Australian years, and Athletics and Manly Sport. For twenty years his influence lifted younger Catholics and the lowly, regardless of any claim but need.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-connolly:
John Connolly was the second Bishop of New York, a Dominican who built churches and charities for his flock. Born at Slane in County Meath in 1750, he joined the Dominicans young, studied at Rome, and held posts as theologian of the Minerva, professor at St. Clement's, agent of the Irish bishops, and prior. He stood high in the esteem of both Pius VI and Pius VII, and his influence saved Irish, Scots, and English colleges from French plunder.

Consecrated at Rome in November 1814, he reached New York a year later. He found a diocese covering New York and part of New Jersey served by four priests. Despite advanced years he worked as bishop and missionary almost to his death in 1825. Churches rose under him, an orphan asylum was founded, and the Sisters of Charity were introduced. He urged dioceses in every state as the best way to advance the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-josef-ru:
Karl Josef Rudolph Cornely was a German biblical scholar and Jesuit, born at Breyell in 1830 and dead at Treves in 1908. He read philosophy and theology at Münster and joined the Society of Jesus in 1852. After philosophy at Paderborn and Bonn and a year of oratory, he taught at Feldkirch from 1857 to 1859. Dogmatic and moral theology at Paderborn preceded his ordination in 1860.

Five years of Scripture study took him through Germany, Ghazir near Beirut, Egypt, and Paris, giving him Syriac, Arabic, Samaritan, and Aramaic. Recalled to Maria-Laach, he became professor of Scripture and Oriental languages there. He edited Stimmen aus Maria-Laach from 1872 to 1879, his clear and vigorous style recalling the German classics. Driven to Tervuren near Brussels by the Jesuits' expulsion in 1872, he kept the periodical at its old level.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-abelly:
Louis Abelly was a French bishop and writer, born in 1603 and dead in 1691. He served as vicar-general of Bayonne, parish priest in Paris, and Bishop of Rodez from 1664, then resigned in 1666 to join St. Vincent de Paul at St. Lazare.

His devotional works show deep, sincere piety, and he fought the Jansenists hard, above all St. Cyran, in his Life of St. Vincent. His Medulla Theologica, praised for solidity and directness, ran through many editions, and Alphonsus calls him a classic on probabilism, the moral rule for doubtful cases. He also wrote guides for bishops and priests and a defence of church hierarchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malachias-o-q:
Malachias O'Queely was Archbishop of Tuam in Ireland. His flock first received him coldly, then soon learned to admire him. He had studied in Paris at the College of Navarre. He administered Killaloe as vicar apostolic. His consecration at Galway came on 11 October 1631.

At Galway in 1632 he held a provincial synod. It spread the decrees of Trent and corrected abuses. His tireless work in Tuam drew a complaint from the Protestant archbishop in 1641. He joined the national synod of 1643 that organised the Catholic Confederation. He sat on its Supreme Council and became President of Connaught. Marching to retake Sligo from Scottish Covenanters in 1645, he was surprised at Ballysodare. He was cut down with his secretary and another priest. His body was ransomed for thirty pounds and buried with solemn rites at Tuam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-de-su:
Maurice de Sully, Bishop of Paris from 1160 to his death in 1196, was born poor at Sully-sur-Loire early in the twelfth century. He reached Paris about 1140, studied for the priesthood, and won fame as a theology teacher and eloquent preacher. In 1159 he appears as Archdeacon of Paris. Largely through Louis VII, he succeeded Peter Lombard as bishop on 12 October 1160.

Notre-Dame Cathedral stands as his monument: building began under him, Alexander III laid its cornerstone in 1163, and the sanctuary was in use by 1185. He also rebuilt the episcopal palace and guarded the royal treasury during the crusade of 1190. A trusted friend of Louis VII and Philip Augustus, he defended Thomas Becket against Henry II in three letters to Alexander III that still survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-o-fih:
Maurice O'Fihely, Archbishop of Tuam, was born about 1460 and died at Galway in 1513. Lynch calls him a native of Clonfert; Ware and Wood say Baltimore in Cork, hence his other name, Maurice a Portu. He studied at Oxford, where he joined the Franciscans, then took a divinity doctorate at Padua and taught philosophy there. A devoted student of Duns Scotus, he wrote a commentary on his works.

At Venice he corrected proofs for the publishers Scott and Locatelli, a task then given only to very learned men. Contemporaries called him Flos Mundi, Flower of the World, for his learning, piety, and skill in affairs. Rome named him Archbishop of Tuam in 1506, and Julius II consecrated him. He attended the first Lateran Council sessions of 1512 but died at Galway in 1513 before reaching his see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-aspects:
Monopoly, by its roots, means exclusive sale. Modern usage stretches it to any unified control of a commodity strong enough to limit supply and fix price. The share needed varies by trade, usually between 70 and 90 per cent, though in some lines just over half suffices. Smaller rivals often prefer the high prices and steady market the dominant firm sets.

Even so, no monopoly's power is absolute. Fear of new rivals, substitutes, or customers doing without the article all restrain it. The entry judges monopoly morally, distinguishing fair gains from extortionate prices. It asks when public authority should act. It weighs the harm to consumers and workers against claims that large combinations bring order and efficiency to an industry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myles-william:
Myles William Patrick O'Reilly, born near Balbriggan in County Dublin on 13 March 1825, was a soldier, publicist and man of letters. He died at Dublin on 2 February 1880. He entered Ushaw College in 1841, graduated from London University, and studied at Rome from 1845 to 1847. He returned to Ireland to aid famine-stricken peasants.

In 1851 he worked with Newman and Archbishop Leahy on the projected Catholic University. In 1854 he became captain of the Louth Rifles. Offering his sword to Pius IX against Garibaldi, he raised an Irish Brigade and fought as major under General Pimodan until Spoleto's surrender in September 1860. He then sat for Longford in Parliament from 1862 to 1876, backing Home Rule, Catholic chaplains for the army, and writing Sufferings for the Faith in Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicosia-sicil:
Nicosia in Sicily, a hill town some 2,800 feet above the sea, stands near salt mines and sulphur springs on the site of ancient Otterbita. Destroyed by Arabs, it rebuilt around a fine cathedral with a rich portal and paintings linked to Velázquez, plus the beautiful church of Santa Maria Maggiore.

Its bishopric dates from 1818 under Cajetan Averna, and the town gave birth to Blessed Felix of Nicosia, a lay Capuchin brother. As a suffragan of Messina, the diocese counts 23 parishes, over 60,000 people, and houses of men and women religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-o-hel:
Patrick O'Hely was Bishop of Mayo, dead at Kilmallock in September 1579. A Connaught native, he joined the Franciscans young, and four years after profession was sent to Alcala University, where he outshone his fellows in sacred studies. Summoned to Rome, he was raised to Mayo in 1576, a see now merged in Tuam, and Gregory XIII empowered him to act in neighbouring dioceses lacking a Catholic bishop.

At Paris he amazed hearers in public disputations with his mastery of Fathers, controversial theology, and Scotist philosophy. In autumn 1579 he sailed from Brittany, landing in Kerry after Fitzmaurice's Smerwick landing, with his companion Conn O'Rourke. Betrayed by the Desmond countess to Limerick's mayor, both churchmen were seized and carried to Kilmallock, where Lord Justice Drury held them, and both died as martyrs for the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-s-cas:
Patrick S. Casserly covers two men in one entry, father and son, both Irish-born scholars and public men. The elder Patrick, an educator dead in New York, ran a classical school there for years and edited the New York Weekly Register. He translated Longinus on the Sublime and Beautiful and Thomas a Kempis's Little Garden of Roses. He edited Jacob's Greek Reader of 1836 through sixteen editions, and wrote a Latin prosody textbook of 1845 still widely used.

His son Eugene Patrick was born in Ireland in 1822 and died at San Francisco on 14 June 1883. He graduated from Georgetown, joined the New York bar in 1844, and served as the city's corporation counsel in 1846 and 1847. Moving to San Francisco in 1850, he took a leading part in local and national politics. He won election as United States senator from California in 1869, and resigned in November 1873 to practise law again.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philipp-johan:
Philipp Johann Gustav von Jolly was a German physicist of hands-on bent, born at Mannheim in 1809. His family had come from France at the century's end. After Mannheim school he studied maths and physics at Heidelberg from 1829. He worked with machines at Vienna in 1832 and 1833, visiting factories and mines, and took his degree at Heidelberg in 1834. He became a professor of maths in 1839 and full professor of physics in 1846.

In 1854 Munich called him to succeed Ohm as physics professor. His work was hands-on, devising new apparatus and improving old forms. Studies of osmosis, gravitation, the earth's density, and the air's makeup produced the Jolly balance of 1864, a special eudiometer of 1879, an improved mercury air-pump, and the Jolly air thermometer. His books covered circular functions, calculus, mechanics, and molecular forces. He died at Munich in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-cally:
Pierre Cally was a French philosopher and theologian, born at Mesnil-Hubert in Normandy, who died on 31 December 1709. He became professor of philosophy and eloquence at Caen in 1660, president of its Collège des Arts in 1675, and parish priest of Saint-Martin in 1684. His philosophy course of 1695 explained and defended Descartes, and he worked zealously to convert Protestants through conferences and books.

His Durand commenté of 1700 denied absolute accidents and replaced transubstantiation with a transformation: the bread's matter remains, becoming the matter of Christ's body. Sixty copies meant for judges became eight hundred printed and sold, sparking fierce debate. On 30 March 1701 Bishop de Nesmond of Bayeux condemned seventeen propositions from the book as false, rash, erroneous, and destructive of the real presence. Cally publicly retracted on 21 April. He also wrote on papal primacy, homilies, and Boethius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-d-aill:
Pierre d'Ailly was a French theologian, philosopher, bishop, and cardinal, born at Compiègne in 1350. At Paris's College of Navarre his 1375 commentaries on Peter Lombard's Sentences advanced Nominalism, and he took his doctorate in 1380. He held that bishops and priests draw jurisdiction from Christ, not the pope, and that a general council stands above the pope. Neither pope nor council, he said, is strictly infallible, only the universal Church.

Director of Navarre in 1384, teacher of Gerson, and chancellor of the university, he became Bishop of Le Puy in 1395 and of Cambrai in 1397. He laboured to end the great schism through a general council. At Constance he presided over the third session in March 1415, urging voting by nations and council power from Christ immediately. His Imago mundi, teaching a western route to the Indies, guided Columbus, who annotated his own copy, now at Seville. He died at Avignon about 1420.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-lully:
Raymond Lully, called Doctor Illuminatus, was a philosopher, poet and theologian, born at Palma in Majorca between 1232 and 1236, and dead at Tunis on 29 June 1315. This encyclopedia entry pictures him as a courtier of King James of Aragon until thirty, then as a hermit and afterwards a tertiary of Saint Francis. From that turn he burned with zeal for converting the Mohammedan world, urging Oriental-language study and the answering of Arabian philosophy, above all Averroes.

He founded a school in Majorca for his community, where Arabic and Chaldean drew attention, and later taught in Paris. About 1291 he reached Tunis, preached to the Saracens and disputed with them in philosophy. After another stay in Paris he returned east as a missionary, enduring many hardships before his death at Tunis. Ribeira, Denifle, De Wulf and Turner supply the entry's sources on a thinker whose missionary fire matched his ambition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sicily:
Sicily, the largest island in the Mediterranean, is triangular in shape and was called Trinacria by the ancients for that reason. It is cut off from the mainland by the Strait of Messina, under two miles wide, and covers 9,935 square miles with its adjacent islands. A northern mountain chain runs from Cape Peloro to Marsala, and near the eastern middle rises Etna, still active, 10,865 feet high, with rich pastures, vineyards, and forests on its slopes.

Greek cities, Roman rule, Vandal and Byzantine masters, and an Arab conquest completed only in 941 after 114 years of war anchor a narrative dominated by history and church history. Monasticism came with Saint Hilarion and grew with exiles from Africa and the East, Greek replaced Latin in many liturgies, and Norman kings later rebuilt the hierarchy. Geography, rivers, lakes, and adjacent island groups complete a full portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-barber-fa:
One family's path from Puritan New England to the Catholic Church anchors this entry, centred on Daniel Barber. Born at Simsbury, Connecticut, in 1756, Barber served two terms as a soldier in the Continental army. He joined the Episcopalians in his late twenties, and was ordained at Schenectady in his thirtieth year. His memoir, History of My Own Times, published in 1827, tells the story in his own voice.

About 1787 he moved with his wife Chloe and their children to Claremont, New Hampshire, where he ministered for thirty years without doubt, as the entry puts it, before turning Catholic. Sons and daughters followed, several into religious life and the priesthood. Their conversions, the entry argues, rippled far beyond one household in early American Catholic history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-drevet-fa:
France's leading portrait engravers for over a century, the Drevets, are the family celebrated here. Fame began with Pierre the Elder, born at Loire in the Lyonnais in 1663, dying at Paris in 1738, son of Estienne Drevet. Germain Audran at Lyons and Gérard Audran at Paris schooled him, and swift progress won him court engraver's place in 1696 and Academy membership in 1707.

Rigaud's portraits, high in favour at the seventeenth century's end, challenged Drevet to render texture and stuffs in black and white as oils showed them. Flesh and fabrics yielded to his graver with precision and delicacy. Son Pierre-Imbert and nephew Claude sustained the fame, carrying the burin through a century of French faces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-stradivar:
Cremona's violin-making name, Stradivari, reaches back to the Middle Ages in this family history. Spellings vary across centuries: Stradivare, Stradiverto, Stradivertus. Fétis finds the name in Cremona's municipal archives for 1127 and 1186. Mandelli cites a May 1188 lease from Cremona cathedral's warden to Giovanni Stradiverto and his heirs as the earliest known mention. 

Learned citizens bore it through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Galiero and Alessandro were Orientalists, Costanzo a monk writing on Aristotle's natural philosophy, and Guglielmus a lawyer who died in 1439. Antonio, the great violin maker, crowns the line, and the entry traces how a common Cremonese name became synonymous with perfect violins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-baily:
Thomas Baily, a Catholic clergyman born in Yorkshire, died at Douai in 1591 after a career shaped by the English Reformation. A fellow of Clare Hall, Cambridge, he became master of the college in 1557 and took a divinity degree the next year. When Elizabeth came to the throne he refused to conform to the new religion and lost his mastership.

He moved to Louvain, took a doctorate in divinity, and then joined Cardinal Allen at Douai and Reims, where he often acted as president of the English College in Allen's absence. Allen handled discipline, Baily managed temporal affairs, and Bristow oversaw studies. Baily was buried in the chapel of St. Nicholas at Douai.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trichinopoly:
A diocese in India, suffragan of Bombay, covering the south-east of the peninsula as far as the Western Ghats. For ease of rule it is split into northern, central and southern districts, centred on Trichinopoly, Madura and Palamcottah, and further divided into fifty-two sections called pangus.

The census of 1907 counted 245,255 Catholics, served by 60 Jesuit priests of the Toulouse province and 19 native secular priests, helped by 156 catechists. A Jesuit novitiate, juniorate and scholasticate stand at Shembaganur, alongside colleges, presses and over a hundred sodalities that show a busy missionary and educational life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-verapoly:
Verapoly is an archdiocese on India's Malabar Coast, stretching from the Ponany River in the north to the Rani in the south. Between the Ghats and the Indian Ocean, with Quilon as suffragan. Its Catholic population divides into two bodies: Thomas Christians of the Syrian rite, under three vicars apostolic, and Latin-rite Catholics, converts of Portuguese missionaries under the archbishop.

The Latin flock numbered about 75,389 souls, served by some ninety priests, including Spanish Carmelite fathers and native secular clergy, with thirty-one churches and twenty-five chapels. Candidates for the priesthood trained at Puttenpally and Kandy. The archbishop lived at Ernakulam, though his cathedral stood at Verapoly, and the entry traces the district's Christian community from its first settlement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-von-worndle-f:
The Wörndle family of Tyrol is treated through its notable members, beginning with Philip von Wörndle of Adelsfried and Weierburg. Major of a Tyrolese rifle corps and militia reserve commandant, born at Hotting-Innsbruck in 1755 and dying at Linz in 1818. Son of a Sonnenburg justice of the peace reinstated in nobility by Maria Theresa in 1763, he took his law doctorate at Innsbruck in 1779, served as judge and advocate.

Married twice, fathering seven children by his first wife. His military career carried him through the Tyrol's wars against France. Under Andreas Hofer in 1809 he was Tyrolese under-commissary and head of national defence for the Puster valley. Later sections follow his brother August and other Wörndles, including a painter of Parzival scenes for Brixen's Vincentinum seminary and Walter von der Vogelweide scenes at Innsbruck's Ferdinandeum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-weld-family:
The Weld family is an ancient English family, conspicuous for zeal for the Church, whose main stem has long settled at Lulworth in Dorsetshire, with branches in England and America. Thomas Weld of Lulworth, 1750 to 1810, distinguished himself relieving French Revolution refugees: he gave Stonyhurst College with thirty acres to the exiled Jesuits.

Besides conspicuous piety and great hospitality, entertaining the king in 1789 and 1791 among the first English Catholics to do so, he steadily supported Bishop Milner. He died without warning at Stonyhurst, where two of his sons also died, one of them its rector, leaving nine sons and six daughters. His eldest, Thomas, cardinal, born in London in 1773 and dying in 1837, continued all his father's liberalities, so that, in Wiseman's words. Scarce a religious establishment in western England lacked some debt of gratitude to him. He stood almost alone for Milner in 1813 when the Catholic committee turned on the bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-croll:
William Crolly was Archbishop of Armagh who raised its cathedral and spread churches and schools across Ulster. Born near Downpatrick in 1780, he died of cholera at Drogheda on Good Friday 1849. With no Catholic schools in the north, he learned classics under a Unitarian minister, entered Maynooth in 1801, topped dogmatic theology in 1806, and took orders that year. He taught logic, metaphysics, and ethics, then ran the vast Belfast parish from 1812.

Named Bishop of Down and Connor in 1825, he moved the episcopal seat to Belfast, built a large church in nearly every parish, and founded Saint Malachy's Seminary. As primate from 1835, he founded Saint Patrick's Seminary at Armagh in 1838 and laid the cathedral foundation stone on Saint Patrick's Day 1840. Famine halted building, and he was buried in the unfinished cathedral choir on Easter Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-monse:
William Monsell, Baron Emly, was an Irish Liberal peer and Catholic spokesman in Parliament. Born in 1812, he died at Tervoe, County Limerick, in 1894. Son of William Monsell of Tervoe, he studied at Winchester and Oriel College, Oxford, leaving without a degree. He inherited the family estates on coming of age as a resident and popular landlord. He married Anna Maria Quin in 1836 and, after her death, Bertha de Martigny in 1857.

Returned for County Limerick in 1847, Monsell sat until 1874 and became a Catholic in 1850. Friend of Wiseman, Newman, Montalembert, and Ward, he pressed Catholic interests in the House to the hierarchy's profit. He served as clerk of the ordnance, privy councillor, vice-president of the Board of Trade, colonial under-secretary, and postmaster-general from 1871 to 1873, entering the peerage as Baron Emly in January 1874. Later opposition to the Land League and Home Rule cost him Irish popularity.
doe-osti-3000611-tomcat5g-a-configuratio:
Patricia Gilfeather and Eric Goodman of Sandia National Laboratories present a 5G analysis tool in report SAND2025-13486R, printed September 2025. Fifth-generation mobile networks are built from software services rather than fixed boxes, so two networks with the same label can differ deeply inside. TOMCAT5G works out, over the air, which features a nearby 5G core actually runs and how far it can be trusted, without joining the network as a normal user.

Three outcomes headline the project. Passive monitoring reads broadcast system information and captured traffic to characterise some core features silently. Active monitoring goes further, using software-defined radios and modified 5G software stacks to send crafted probes that fully classify the core type. A third thread uses radio techniques to give devices extra location privacy. The team expects the passive and active pieces to merge into one larger tool, with follow-on work on network resilience.
doe-osti-3012820-role-of-electrolyte-in-:
University of Rhode Island chemist Brett Lucht is the contact for this short DOE research summary on why high-voltage lithium ion batteries lose capacity. The work, published in ACS Energy Letters in 2021 by Chamithri Jayawardhana and co-authors, challenges the usual blame placed on transition metals dissolving from the cathode. Instead it points at acid formed when the electrolyte oxidizes.

The team measured difluorophosphoric acid, a strong acid generated at the cathode, for two cathode materials using fluorine NMR. Acid levels tracked closely with damage to the anode's protective film and with capacity loss. The summary suggests fixes worth testing, such as electrolyte recipes or cathode coatings that block the oxidation step. The award behind the work was DE-SC0021392.
doe-osti-3364328-suli-intern-final-repor:
A SULI intern final report from August 2025 records Alison Jensen's project at Idaho National Laboratory, mentored by Jackson Harter. The University of Wyoming student used computer modeling to study how hydrogen moves through yttrium hydride when temperature varies across the material. Yttrium hydride serves as a neutron moderator in compact reactor designs, and hydrogen drifting toward hot or cold zones changes how the moderator performs.

Methods spanned scales: quantum-level static and nudged elastic band calculations mapped the energy barriers hydrogen atoms hop over, molecular dynamics watched the motion directly, and phonon calculations supplied heat-related properties. Mesoscale models then carried the atomic results upward. Three diffusion cases through the crystal's tetrahedral sites anchor the nanoscale results. The project shows how multiscale simulation can predict a safety-relevant drift effect without hot laboratory experiments.
doe-osti-3400807-savy-4000-finite-elemen:
Timothy Marion Jude Lyons of Los Alamos group E-13 reports a finite-element drop test analysis of the SAVY-4000 in LA-UR-26-27012, issued August 5, 2026. The SAVY-4000 is a container for storing nuclear material. Drop testing is its accident case: if a loaded container falls, the body and seals must hold.
